Clinical Reference

Inpatient Diabetes Management

On this page
Hospital hyperglycemia is any inpatient glucose >140 mg/dL — and the job is not "cover the sugars," it is to build a scheduled insulin plan (basal + prandial + correction) matched to what the patient is actually eating, then titrate it daily and hand off a safe regimen at discharge.
Ward goal 100–180 mg/dL (ADA 2026 §16.5b) ICU goal 140–180 mg/dL (§16.5a) Start insulin at BG ≥180 ×2 in 24 h Sliding-scale ALONE is discouraged — Grade A Starting TDD 0.3–0.6 U/kg/day 50% basal / 50% prandial
Shared

Pathophysiology

🧬

Why hospitalized people run high — the story

Normally the β-cell of the pancreatic islet is a thermostat: it senses glucose entering through GLUT2, generates ATP, closes the KATP channel, depolarizes, lets calcium in, and releases insulin. Insulin then does two things — it tells the liver to stop making glucose (suppresses gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis) and tells muscle and fat to take glucose up (translocates GLUT4 to the membrane). Basal insulin secretion, running quietly between meals, exists almost entirely to hold the liver's output in check; the sharp prandial spikes exist to clear the carbohydrate of a meal.

Acute illness attacks both arms of that system at once. Sepsis, trauma, surgery, myocardial infarction, and pain all trigger a counterregulatory hormone surge — cortisol, catecholamines, glucagon, and growth hormone — plus inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6). Cortisol and glucagon drive hepatic glucose production up; catecholamines add glycogenolysis and directly suppress insulin release; TNF-α and IL-6 phosphorylate insulin-receptor substrate-1 on serine residues, which uncouples the receptor from its downstream signal and blocks GLUT4 from reaching the cell surface. The result is a liver pouring out glucose into muscle that has stopped accepting it. Layer on iatrogenic fuel — glucocorticoids, dextrose-containing fluids, continuous tube feeds, TPN — and the glucose has nowhere to go.

This is why the inpatient problem is fundamentally different from clinic diabetes. In clinic you are treating a slow, stable defect over months. In the hospital you are treating a moving target: insulin requirements can double when steroids start and halve when they stop, when the patient goes NPO, when sepsis resolves, or when the kidneys fail and stop clearing insulin. A regimen that was correct yesterday can cause hypoglycemia today. That is the single most important idea in this guide.

Think of basal insulin as the thermostat and prandial insulin as opening a window when you cook. Sliding-scale-only insulin is neither: it is running to the window and flinging it open after the kitchen has already filled with smoke, then closing it, then waiting for the smoke again. It is a reactive loop that never sets the baseline — which is exactly why RABBIT-2 showed it loses.

Figure 1 — Two hits produce inpatient hyperglycemia: the liver over-produces (basal insulin's job) while muscle and fat under-consume (prandial insulin's job). Every drug in this guide is aimed at one of those two arrows.
A pancreatic islet: insulin-producing β-cells and glucagon-producing α-cells. Inpatient hyperglycemia is a failure of this unit to out-shout the stress hormones.
Jakob Suckale, Michele Solimena — CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons: Suckale08 fig2 islet structure.jpg
Pancreatic anatomy and histology — the endocrine islets are a tiny fraction (~1–2%) of pancreatic mass but set whole-body glucose flux.
Paoli C, Carrer A — CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons: Anatomy and histology of the pancreas.png
The whole guide in one sentence: basal insulin answers the liver (needed whether or not the patient eats — never hold it in type 1 diabetes); prandial/nutritional insulin answers the carbohydrate load (hold it when the carbohydrate stops); correction insulin is a small top-up that fixes the error the other two made, and it can never do their job alone.

Three glycemic phenotypes you will meet on admission

PhenotypeHow to recognize itAdmission A1cWhat it changes
Known diabetesDocumented history, home glucose-lowering medsAny value; reflects pre-admission controlStart from the home regimen (usually ~80% of home insulin dose); discharge plan is a modification of what they came in on
Undiagnosed diabetesHyperglycemia in hospital, no history — but A1c ≥6.5%≥6.5% (≥48 mmol/mol) means the diabetes preceded the admissionThis is a new chronic diagnosis. They need a real outpatient regimen, education, and follow-up — not just an inpatient scale
Stress hyperglycemia
(hospital-related)		Hyperglycemia in hospital, no history, A1c <6.5%<6.5% — glycemia was normal before this illnessOften resolves as the illness and steroids resolve. Treat while high, then taper off. Still needs outpatient re-screening — it marks future diabetes risk

This is exactly why ADA 2026 §16.1 (Grade B) says to send an A1c on admission for every patient with diabetes or a random glucose >140 mg/dL if there is no result from the prior 3 months — one $15 test sorts the three phenotypes above and tells you what the discharge regimen should be.

Beware the arithmetic trap: A1c reflects the last ~3 months, so it tells you about the outpatient, not today's ward glucose. And it is unreliable in exactly the patients you see in hospital — falsely low with recent transfusion, acute blood loss, hemolysis, or advanced CKD/EPO use (young red cells), and falsely high with iron-deficiency anemia or uremia. When A1c and the glucose pattern disagree, believe the glucose.

onset · peak · duration

Almost every inpatient insulin error is a timing error, not a dose error. Learn the curve for each insulin and the errors stop.

📊

Who has it, what you see, and why

frequency + mechanism

The defining clinical feature of inpatient hyperglycemia is that it is usually silent. Nobody complains of a glucose of 260. You find it because you checked. That is why protocolized point-of-care testing — not symptoms — is the case-finding tool.

A. Epidemiology — the numbers that justify a protocol

Finding~FrequencyWhy it happens / why it matters
Hyperglycemia at hospital admission (BG >126 fasting or >200 random, ×2)38%Combined effect of a high background diabetes prevalence plus the counterregulatory surge of acute illness. Of 2,030 consecutive admissions, 38% were hyperglycemic (Umpierrez, JCEM 2002).
— of whom had known diabetes26% of all admissionsDiabetes drives admission (infection, CAD, CKD, foot disease) and is worsened by it — a bidirectional loop.
— of whom had newly recognized hyperglycemia12% of all admissionsMix of true undiagnosed diabetes (A1c ≥6.5%) and pure stress hyperglycemia (A1c <6.5%). The admission A1c is what separates them.
In-hospital mortality — new hyperglycemia16%vs 3% with known diabetes and 1.7% with normoglycemia. Newly high glucose is largely a marker of illness severity — but it also flags a patient with no glycemic reserve and no established plan.
Diabetes among patients having major general surgeryup to 20%Surgical stress + fasting + anesthesia + post-op steroids/pressors. Perioperative hyperglycemia independently predicts surgical site infection (ADA 2026).
Prediabetes or undiagnosed diabetes in surgical patients23–60%Wide range reflects differing screening thresholds across studies. Pre-op is a high-yield screening moment.
Hospitalized patients on ongoing glucocorticoids10–15%Oncology, COPD/asthma, autoimmune disease, transplant, COVID-era protocols.
Hyperglycemia among steroid-treated inpatients56–86%Glucocorticoids raise hepatic glucose output and block peripheral uptake — the single most predictable iatrogenic cause on the wards. Occurs with or without preexisting diabetes.
Hypoglycemia (<70 mg/dL) on a full basal-bolus regimen16%The honest cost of scheduled insulin (Basal Plus trial). Severe hypoglycemia (<40) was not increased vs sliding scale — the trade is mild lows for far better control.
Severe hypoglycemia (<40 mg/dL) preceded by an earlier low (<70) in the same admission84%The single most actionable statistic in this guide: severe hypoglycemia is almost never a bolt from the blue. It is a missed warning. This is why ADA §16.13 makes reviewing the regimen mandatory after any value <70.
Hypoglycemic episodes (<50 mg/dL) occurring in patients on basal insulin78%Basal excess is the dominant mechanism, and the peak incidence is midnight–6 AM when nobody is eating. Yet 75% of these patients had no change to the next basal dose.
Treatment failure on sliding-scale-only insulin
(>2 consecutive BG >240 or mean daily BG >240)		19%vs 0% on basal-bolus and 2% on basal-plus-correction (Basal Plus trial). One in five patients on a scale alone simply never gets controlled.
Hyperglycemic crisis (DKA/HHS) as the reason for admission in people with diabetes~1% of their hospitalizationsUncommon as a proportion but high-acuity. Covered in the dedicated DKA and HHS guides.

B. Symptoms and signs — and why they mislead you here

Frequencies below are approximate clinical estimates for hospitalized adults with hyperglycemia (not trial-derived), because symptom prevalence is not systematically reported in the inpatient literature. They are shown to teach the pattern, not to be quoted as data.

Symptom / sign~FrequencyMechanism — why it happens
None — asymptomatic, found on POC glucose>70%Symptoms need sustained glucose above the renal threshold (~180–200 mg/dL) for hours. Most ward hyperglycemia is intermittent and post-prandial, and acute illness masks the rest.
Polyuria / nocturia40–60% when BG persistently >250Filtered glucose exceeds proximal tubular SGLT2 reabsorptive capacity → glucose stays in tubular fluid → osmotic diuresis drags water and Na⁺/K⁺ with it. Easily blamed on IV fluids or diuretics.
Polydipsia / thirst40–60%Hypertonicity from hyperglycemia pulls water out of cells and stimulates hypothalamic osmoreceptors. Blunted in the elderly and absent in anyone NPO, sedated, or delirious — the exact patients at highest risk.
Fatigue / malaise40–60%Cells cannot take up glucose without insulin signalling; add volume depletion and electrolyte loss. Almost always attributed to the admitting illness instead.
Blurred vision15–30%Osmotic swelling of the lens changes refractive index. Fluctuates with glucose — never prescribe new glasses to an inpatient with uncontrolled sugars.
Volume depletion (dry mucosa, orthostasis, rising creatinine)15–35%Direct consequence of the osmotic diuresis above. Often the finding that first flags how long the glucose has been high.
Poor wound healing / surgical site infection~10–25% (wound infection 10.3% on SSI vs 2.9% on basal-bolus, RABBIT-2 Surgery)Hyperglycemia impairs neutrophil chemotaxis, phagocytosis and oxidative burst, glycates complement, and reduces collagen deposition. The measured, trial-level cost of bad inpatient control.
Altered mental status<10%Requires marked hypertonicity — think HHS (effective osm >300 mOsm/kg) — or hypoglycemia. In an inpatient on insulin, check a glucose before you assume anything else.
Kussmaul respiration, abdominal pain, vomiting, fruity breath<5%Ketoacidosis, not simple hyperglycemia. Insulin deficiency → lipolysis → hepatic ketogenesis → anion-gap acidosis with respiratory compensation. Different disease, different guide.
Any inpatient with an unexplained change in mental status gets a fingerstick glucose before a head CT, before naloxone, before anything. Hypoglycemia is the most rapidly reversible and most frequently missed cause of inpatient encephalopathy, and its classic adrenergic warning signs (tremor, sweating, palpitations) are silenced by β-blockers, by sedation, and by recurrent lows.

Assess

The home regimen you inherit

🏠

What to ask before you write a single order

The admission history for a patient with diabetes is not "do you take insulin?" It is a short, specific interrogation, because every answer changes the inpatient plan. Ask, and document:

Type of diabetesType 1 vs type 2 vs pancreatogenic (type 3c) vs steroid-induced. Type 1 changes everything: basal insulin can never be held, even NPO, or they go into DKA within hours. Clues to type 1: diagnosed young/lean, on a pump, prior DKA, on basal+bolus with small doses, positive antibodies, C-peptide low. Pancreatogenic (post-pancreatectomy, chronic pancreatitis, CF) is brittle — glucagon deficiency too, so hypoglycemia is severe and prolonged.Always
Exact insulin names, doses, times"Lantus 32 units at bedtime, Humalog 8-8-10 with meals" — not "insulin." Get the units and the time of the last dose. A basal given 4 h ago is still fully on board; degludec given 2 days ago is still on board.Always
Actual adherencePrescribed dose ≠ taken dose. If they have been skipping insulin for a month because of cost, restarting the full home dose will cause hypoglycemia. ADA 2026 explicitly says the decision to restart the home plan must account for how the patient was actually using it.Always
Non-insulin agentsMetformin, sulfonylurea, SGLT2 inhibitor, GLP-1/GIP receptor agonist, DPP-4 inhibitor, TZD. Ask specifically about SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 agonists — both change acute management (euglycemic DKA; aspiration risk) and both are frequently taken for weight or heart failure, so patients may not list them as "diabetes pills."Always
DevicesInsulin pump? Automated insulin delivery (AID/hybrid closed-loop)? CGM? Note the make. Under ADA 2026 §16.6/§16.7 these are continued when clinically appropriate and the patient can self-manage — but you need a documented plan and institutional policy.Always
Hypoglycemia historyAny severe episode (needing help) in the last year? Any hypoglycemia unawareness? Both mandate a more permissive inpatient target and a lower starting dose.Always
Kidney function & recent weighteGFR drives both insulin clearance and which oral agents can continue. Weight drives the whole weight-based dose calculation.Always
A1c in the last 3 monthsIf none, order it now — ADA 2026 §16.1, Grade B. It sorts the three phenotypes and directly determines the discharge regimen.Admit
Two questions catch most of the danger: "When exactly did you take your last dose?" and "Have you been eating normally?" A patient who has been vomiting for two days and took full basal this morning is a hypoglycemia event waiting to happen, no matter how high their glucose is right now.
Med rec

Which home agents to hold — and why

⛔

Non-insulin agents on admission

the default is HOLD

ADA 2026 and the Endocrine Society 2022 guideline agree: insulin is the preferred inpatient therapy (Endo Society Rec 7.1), and most oral/injectable agents come off on admission. Not because they are bad drugs — because their pharmacology assumes a stable, eating, hemodynamically normal outpatient, and a hospitalized patient is none of those things. Each one fails in a specific and predictable way:

Agent classDefaultExactly why it fails inpatientWhen it can continue
MetforminHOLD Metformin is renally cleared and inhibits hepatic mitochondrial complex I; if it accumulates (AKI, shock, sepsis, hypoxia) lactate cannot be consumed by gluconeogenesis and you get metformin-associated lactic acidosis — rare (~1–9 per 100,000 patient-years) but with high mortality. It is also useless acutely: no rapid glucose-lowering, and it causes GI upset in someone already nauseated. Consider continuing only in a stable, eating, non-septic patient with stable eGFR ≥45, no contrast planned, no AKI. Reduce dose at eGFR 30–45; stop at eGFR <30. Hold on the day of any surgery or procedure (ADA 2026). For iodinated contrast, current ACR guidance holds metformin for 48 h with re-check of renal function only if eGFR <30, if AKI is suspected, or for intra-arterial contrast with likely renal exposure — the old blanket 48 h hold for everyone is obsolete.
SGLT2 inhibitors
empagliflozin, dapagliflozin, canagliflozin, ertugliflozin		HOLD (with one big exception) Euglycemic DKA. By dumping glucose in the urine they lower glucose and insulin levels while raising glucagon — so lipolysis and ketogenesis proceed with a glucose that may be under 200 mg/dL. Fasting, surgery, and acute illness are exactly the triggers. They also cause volume depletion and can worsen AKI. Note: ~10% of all DKA is euglycemic (ADA 2026), and the anion gap, not the glucose, makes the diagnosis. ADA 2026 §16.11 (Grade A): initiate or continue an SGLT2 inhibitor if indicated for heart failure, absent contraindications, after recovery from the acute illness. Avoid in severe illness, ketonemia/ketonuria, or prolonged fasting. Hold 3–4 days before elective surgery (FDA: at least 3 days; 4 days for ertugliflozin). Adjust insulin and diuretics proactively when restarting.
Sulfonylureas
glipizide, glyburide, glimepiride		HOLD They close the KATP channel and force insulin release regardless of whether the patient eats — a fixed, long-acting secretagogue in a patient with unpredictable intake, procedures, and NPO periods. Glyburide has an active renally-cleared metabolite and causes prolonged, recurrent hypoglycemia in CKD. There is no dose that is safe when meals are unreliable. Essentially never inpatient. If a sulfonylurea overdose/hypoglycemia occurs, treat with dextrose and consider octreotide (suppresses the ongoing insulin release) — plain dextrose alone provokes more insulin secretion and rebound lows.
Meglitinides
repaglinide, nateglinide		HOLD Same KATP mechanism, shorter acting — meant to be taken with each meal and skipped when the meal is skipped. That coordination almost never survives a hospital tray schedule. No inpatient role. Replace with scheduled prandial insulin.
Thiazolidinediones
pioglitazone, rosiglitazone		HOLD PPAR-γ agonists take weeks to work — zero acute benefit — and cause sodium and fluid retention, which precipitates or worsens heart failure and peripheral edema in exactly the population being admitted. No acute role. Reassess at discharge; avoid entirely in HFrEF/NYHA III–IV.
GLP-1 & dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonists
semaglutide, dulaglutide, liraglutide, tirzepatide, exenatide		HOLD in acutely ill patients (ADA 2026) Nausea, vomiting and delayed gastric emptying in someone who already can't eat — and case reports of pulmonary aspiration under general anesthesia/deep sedation prompted an FDA label warning on the whole class. Retrospective data show increased residual gastric content despite fasting, and one study found this even when semaglutide was held for an average of 10 days (up to 30). ADA 2026 endorses a personalized perioperative approach rather than a fixed hold: weigh the indication, dose/duration, GI symptoms, and procedure type. Options include a 24 h clear-liquid protocol pre-procedure, pre-op gastric ultrasound, or full-stomach precautions if symptomatic. The older ASA advice (hold day-of for daily agents, ≥7 days for weekly) is now considered too blunt. If you hold it and glycemia worsens, cover with insulin.
DPP-4 inhibitors
sitagliptin, linagliptin, saxagliptin, alogliptin		May continue / may start The one class with real inpatient evidence. They only amplify glucose-dependent incretin signalling, so they essentially cannot cause hypoglycemia on their own. Weak (~0.5–0.8% A1c equivalent) — they cannot rescue a glucose of 350. Sita-Hospital (n=277) showed sitagliptin + once-daily glargine was non-inferior to full basal-bolus (mean BG 171 vs 169 mg/dL; treatment failure 16% vs 19%; hypoglycemia 9% vs 12%) in non-ICU medicine/surgery patients. Endo Society Rec 7.2: reasonable for mild hyperglycemia with A1c <7.5% and prior insulin <0.6 U/kg/day. ADA 2026: consider when admission glucose <180–200 mg/dL. Renal dosing: sitagliptin 100 → 50 → 25 mg by declining eGFR; linagliptin needs no renal adjustment — the easy choice in CKD. FDA advises considering stopping saxagliptin and alogliptin in patients who develop heart failure.
Home insulinCONTINUE — modified Endo Society Rec 10.3 is the guideline's only STRONG recommendation: continue the scheduled insulin regimen, modified for nutritional status and severity of illness. Stopping insulin in type 1 diabetes causes DKA; stopping it in insulin-requiring type 2 causes runaway hyperglycemia. See the Wards panel for exactly how much to reduce and when.
Drugs to avoid or use with extreme caution in the hospitalized patient with diabetes
  • Glyburide — active renally-cleared metabolite; prolonged hypoglycemia in any CKD. If a sulfonylurea must be used at all, glipizide is the least renally dependent.
  • Any SGLT2 inhibitor during fasting, severe illness, or within 3–4 days of surgery — euglycemic DKA presents with a normal glucose and a wide anion gap; it is missed precisely because the sugar looks fine.
  • Premixed insulins (70/30, 75/25, 50/50) — a fixed basal:prandial ratio cannot be unbundled when the patient goes NPO. Randomized inpatient data show significantly more hypoglycemia vs basal-bolus. Convert on admission.
  • Correction-only ("sliding scale") insulin as sole therapy — ADA 2026 §16.10, Grade A: discouraged. Absolutely contraindicated in type 1 diabetes.
  • Non-selective β-blockers — mask the adrenergic warning symptoms of hypoglycemia and blunt the glycogenolytic recovery response. Cardioselective agents are preferred but do not fully avoid this.
  • Fluoroquinolones (esp. moxifloxacin, gatifloxacin) — dysglycemia via KATP channel effects; can cause both hypo- and hyperglycemia, worse with concomitant sulfonylureas or CKD.
  • Octreotide — suppresses insulin and glucagon and growth hormone; usually hyperglycemia, occasionally hypoglycemia. Unpredictable — check glucose more often after starting.
  • Pentamidine — direct β-cell cytotoxicity: an early hypoglycemic phase from insulin dumping, then permanent hyperglycemia.
  • U-500 insulin and concentrated basals inpatient — ten-fold dosing errors. Pharmacy-drawn or pen only; consult endocrine.

Hospital drugs that will push the glucose up on you

When the glucose suddenly worsens on day 3, the answer is usually on the medication list, not the pancreas.

AgentMechanismWhat to do
Glucocorticoids↑ hepatic gluconeogenesis, ↓ peripheral GLUT4, ↓ insulin secretionAnticipate — see the dedicated steroid module in Wards. Expect prandial/correction needs to rise 40–60% or more at high doses.
Tacrolimus > cyclosporineDirect calcineurin-mediated β-cell toxicity → post-transplant diabetesTrend levels; hyperglycemia is dose-related and may improve as levels come down.
Vasopressors / catecholamines (norepinephrine, epinephrine, dobutamine)β₂-mediated glycogenolysis + α₂-mediated suppression of insulin releaseInsulin requirement falls sharply as pressors wean — a classic cause of ICU hypoglycemia.
Dextrose-containing IV fluids & citrate/dialysateDirect carbohydrate delivery, often unnoticedCount D5/D10 as nutrition. Peritoneal dialysate is a major hidden glucose load.
Enteral feeds and TPNContinuous carbohydrate infusion = a continuous post-prandial stateRequires its own insulin strategy — see the NPO/feeds module.
Atypical antipsychotics (olanzapine, clozapine > quetiapine)Weight gain + direct insulin resistance and impaired secretionMonitor; matters most for the discharge regimen.
Thiazides, protease inhibitors, interferon, niacin, checkpoint inhibitorsVaried: ↓K⁺-mediated insulin secretion (thiazide); GLUT4 inhibition (PIs); autoimmune β-cell destruction (checkpoint inhibitors — can cause fulminant, DKA-presenting type 1 diabetes)Checkpoint-inhibitor diabetes is a true endocrine emergency — abrupt onset, insulin-dependent forever, does not respond to steroids.

Do not apply outpatient targets to an inpatient. Chasing 80–130 mg/dL on a ward patient with unpredictable intake is how you generate the 3 AM hypoglycemia that kills the whole plan. The inpatient goals are deliberately looser: 100–180 mg/dL on the floor, 140–180 in the ICU.

2
Add basal insulin — the step most relevant to your discharge order
Start low, titrate by fasting glucose
▾
10 U (or 0.1–0.2 U/kg) at bedtime→↑ 2 U every 3 days→while fasting BG >130→reassess at >0.5 U/kg/day — add prandial instead of pushing basal higher

Titrate to the fasting glucose, not the A1c. Back off 10–20% for any hypoglycemia. The classic error — "over-basalization" — is escalating basal past ~0.5 U/kg/day to fix post-meal numbers; that produces overnight lows without fixing the daytime peaks. When the fasting glucose is at goal but the day is high, the answer is prandial insulin or a GLP-1 RA, not more basal.

3
Full basal-bolus / intensification
Add prandial insulin, largest meal first
▾

Add rapid-acting insulin 4 U or 10% of the basal dose before the largest meal ("basal plus"), titrate by 1–2 U every 3 days to the next pre-meal glucose, then extend to the other meals as needed. This is the outpatient mirror of the inpatient basal-plus strategy validated in the Basal Plus trial.

Discharge

The discharge regimen & follow-up

📤

Choosing the regimen by admission A1c

ADA 2026 §16.18

ADA 2026 §16.18 (Grade B) requires a structured discharge plan, and notes that a discharge algorithm based on admission A1c, pre-admission medications, and inpatient insulin use guides treatment decisions and significantly improves post-discharge A1c. This is the practical version of that algorithm — the admission A1c you sent on day 1 is what makes it work.

Admission A1cWhat it tells youDischarge regimenFollow-up
<7%Pre-admission control was good. The hyperglycemia was the illness, not the regimen.Resume the home regimen unchanged. Restart held oral agents once eating, hemodynamically stable, and renal function has returned to baseline. Do not send them home on hospital insulin doses.Routine — but still within 1 month.
7–9%Control was drifting before admission. The regimen needs to be stronger, but not rebuilt.Resume the home regimen PLUS add basal insulin at roughly 50–80% of the basal dose that worked in hospital — or intensify the oral/GLP-1 regimen. Reduce because home activity, appetite and stress differ from the ward.1–2 weeks (medications changed).
>9%The outpatient regimen has failed. Sending them out on it guarantees readmission.Discharge on basal-bolus insulin, or basal + oral agents, at ~80–100% of the effective inpatient dose. These patients need real education, supplies, and early contact.1–2 weeks, plus consider a diabetes-educator or endocrinology referral before discharge.

ADA 2026: an outpatient visit with primary care, endocrinology, or a diabetes care and education specialist within 1 month is advised for everyone who had hyperglycemia or hypoglycemia in hospital; if medications were changed or control is not optimal at discharge, an appointment at 1–2 weeks is preferred.

Restarting held agents — the safe sequence. Metformin: only once creatinine is back to baseline, the patient is eating, hemodynamically stable, and ≥48 h past contrast if it was held for that. SGLT2 inhibitor: only when nutritional intake has resumed and any ketosis has fully resolved — and per §16.11 restart it deliberately if the indication is heart failure, adjusting insulin and diuretics at the same time. Sulfonylurea: restart at a reduced dose, or not at all, if renal function is worse than on admission or the patient had any inpatient hypoglycemia. GLP-1 RA: restart when eating reliably; if they missed >2 weekly doses, re-titrate from a lower dose to avoid severe nausea.

The discharge checklist — AHRQ minimum, per ADA 2026

Medication reconciliationCross-check home vs hospital lists: nothing chronic silently stopped, no duplicate under a different brand name (Lantus/Basaglar/Semglee are the same insulin), new prescriptions filled and reviewed before discharge.Required
Supplies & devicesInsulin, pen needles or syringes (the most commonly forgotten item — an insulin prescription without needles is useless), glucometer + test strips + lancets or CGM sensors, sharps container, glucagon rescue for anyone on insulin or a sulfonylurea.Required
EducationInjection technique and site rotation, glucose monitoring and home targets, hypoglycemia recognition and the 15-15 rule, sick-day rules (never stop basal insulin when ill; check glucose and ketones more often), safe disposal, and who to call.Required
Structured communicationDischarge summary to the PCP promptly, stating medication changes, pending tests, the root cause of the hyperglycemia (or the plan to find it), and the recommended follow-up.Required
Appointment booked before they leaveScheduled with the patient agreeing to the time and place — ADA notes this measurably increases attendance.Required
Cost & access checkAsk what the insulin will cost them. A perfect regimen they cannot afford is a readmission. Human insulin (NPH + regular) is a legitimate, far cheaper fallback if analogs are unaffordable — accept the slightly higher hypoglycemia risk and teach the timing.High yield
If not going homeADA 2026 added this in 2026: consider the facility's capabilities. Many SNFs cannot do 4-times-daily glucose checks or complex correction scales. Simplify to a regimen the receiving facility can actually execute — often basal + a single simple correction scale.New 2026
If the patient experienced DKA or HHS this admission, ADA §16.17 (Grade B) makes discharge education on recognizing, preventing and managing it mandatory — recurrence and readmission are common, and 1-year age-corrected mortality after a DKA admission is 13× the general population.
Prevent

USPSTF A/B & prevention

🛡️

Grade A & B recommendations relevant to this population

GradeRecommendationPopulation
BScreen for prediabetes and type 2 diabetes, and offer or refer patients with prediabetes to effective preventive interventionsAdults 35–70 years with overweight or obesity (BMI ≥25). Repeat every 3 years if normal.
BStatin for primary prevention of cardiovascular diseaseAdults 40–75 with ≥1 CVD risk factor (diabetes counts) and 10-year risk ≥10%.
BScreen for hypertensionAdults ≥18; confirm outside the clinical setting before starting treatment.
BOffer intensive behavioral counseling for a healthy diet and physical activityAdults with CVD risk factors — including diabetes.
AScreen for tobacco use and provide cessation interventionsAll adults; smoking multiplies microvascular and macrovascular diabetic complications.
BScreen for obesity and offer/refer to intensive multicomponent behavioral interventionsAdults with BMI ≥30.

USPSTF grades A and B only, per current USPSTF recommendation statements (uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org). USPSTF does not issue an inpatient glycemic-management recommendation; the inpatient standards come from ADA and the Endocrine Society.

Disease-specific prevention that belongs in the discharge summary

  • Vaccines: influenza annually; COVID-19 per current schedule; pneumococcal per age/risk schedule; hepatitis B for unvaccinated adults with diabetes; RSV and zoster per age criteria. Hospitalization is a capture opportunity.
  • Annual complication screening: dilated retinal exam, urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio + eGFR, comprehensive foot exam with monofilament testing.
  • ACE inhibitor or ARB if albuminuria or hypertension; statin per risk; SGLT2 inhibitor for CKD or heart failure regardless of A1c.
Diabetic retinopathy — dot-blot hemorrhages and hard exudates. Chronic complications are why the inpatient stay matters: it is often the only healthcare contact of the year.

Escalate

When to send them in

🚑

Red flags → ED / admission

Send to the ED now:
  • Suspected DKA — glucose ≥200 mg/dL (or known diabetes) plus β-hydroxybutyrate ≥3.0 mmol/L or urine ketones ≥2+ plus pH <7.3 and/or bicarbonate <18 mmol/L. All three criteria required (ADA 2026 Table 16.1). Remember ~10% is euglycemic (glucose <200) — think of it in anyone on an SGLT2 inhibitor, pregnant, fasting, or with liver failure.
  • Suspected HHS — glucose ≥600 mg/dL, effective serum osmolality >300 mOsm/kg, β-hydroxybutyrate <3.0 mmol/L, pH ≥7.3 and bicarbonate ≥15 mmol/L, usually with altered cognition.
  • Any severe (level 3) hypoglycemia requiring another person's help — especially on a sulfonylurea (long-acting; will recur for 24–72 h and needs observation, not just a juice box) or with a large basal insulin dose.
  • Persistent vomiting or inability to keep fluids down in a patient on insulin — they cannot safely take their insulin and cannot rehydrate; this is the classic path into DKA.
  • Hyperglycemia with a serious infection — necrotizing soft-tissue infection, foot ulcer with deep probing/bone contact or systemic signs, pyelonephritis with sepsis physiology.
  • Marked hyperglycemia with volume depletion or a rising creatinine — glucose >400–500 mg/dL with orthostasis or an AKI is not an outpatient titration problem.
  • New severe hyperglycemia with weight loss and ketones in a lean or young patient — new type 1 diabetes, or checkpoint-inhibitor-induced diabetes. Do not send them home on metformin.
Every patient on an SGLT2 inhibitor who feels unwell needs a ketone check, not a glucose check. Euglycemic DKA is the one diagnosis where the fingerstick reassures you and the anion gap convicts you. Check β-hydroxybutyrate and a basic metabolic panel.
🛏️ Wards — the core of inpatient glucose management

Glycemic targets & when to start insulin

🎯

Read the two targets carefully — they are not the same, and this trips up residents. The ICU goal is 140–180. The ward goal in the 2026 Standards is 100–180 — a lower floor, permitted because floor patients are eating, awake, able to report symptoms, and not on a titrated drip. The qualifier "if it can be achieved without significant hypoglycemia" is doing real work: in a frail 88-year-old with an eGFR of 22, 140–180 remains the right target and many institutional order sets still use it. Know both, and know why.

When to individualize — and in which direction

SituationTargetReasoning
Most medical/surgical ward patients, eating, stable100–180 mg/dLADA 2026 §16.5b default.
Selected critically ill, e.g. post-cardiac surgery110–140 mg/dL may be reasonable§16.5a allows more stringent goals if achievable without significant hypoglycemia. GLUCO-CABG found no overall benefit of 100–140 vs 141–180 post-CABG (composite complications 42% vs 52%, P=0.08) — but in the non-diabetic subgroup, tighter control did reduce complications (34% vs 55%, P=0.008).
Advanced CKD / on dialysisRelax — up to 200–250Insulin is cleared by the kidney; as eGFR falls insulin half-life rises and hypoglycemia risk climbs steeply. Kidney failure is an independent risk factor for inpatient hypoglycemia (ADA 2026).
Terminal illness / comfort-focused goals / short life expectancyRelax — avoid symptoms only (keep <250–300)The goal becomes preventing osmotic symptoms and hypoglycemia, not preventing complications that will never develop. Consider stopping fingersticks and correction insulin entirely.
Hypoglycemia unawareness or any prior severe episodeRelax the lower bound; target 140–180Impaired counterregulation means the next low will be more severe and less heralded.
On continuous enteral or parenteral nutritionDo not push below 140ADA 2026 is explicit: because continuous feeds create a continuous post-prandial state, driving glucose below 140 "substantially increases the risk of hypoglycemia" — the feed can stop at any moment while the insulin keeps working.
PregnancySubstantially tighter — manage with OB/endocrineDifferent physiology and different targets; out of scope here. Involve maternal-fetal medicine.
A fasting glucose <100 mg/dL is not a victory — it is a warning. ADA 2026 cites data showing a fasting glucose under 100 predicts hypoglycemia within the next 24 hours, and states it "necessitates basal insulin dose adjustments." Treat a fasting 92 on the floor as a signal to cut basal by 10–20%, not as a job well done.
Orders

Admission order set

🧪

Labs, monitoring & imaging — with the trigger for each

POC glucoseEating: before each meal + at bedtime (4×/day). Not eating / NPO / continuous feeds: every 4–6 h. On IV insulin: every 30 min to 2 h. Order the "meal triad" — glucose check, tray delivery and nutritional insulin must be coordinated; uncoupling them is a leading cause of both hyper- and hypoglycemia (ADA 2026).Admit
Hemoglobin A1cOn every patient with diabetes or a random glucose >140 mg/dL, if no result in the prior 3 months — §16.1, Grade B. It classifies the phenotype and sets the discharge regimen. Interpret with caution in anemia, hemolysis, recent transfusion, CKD, or pregnancy.Admit
Basic metabolic panelAdmission and daily while insulin is being titrated. Watch K⁺ (insulin drives it intracellularly — a normal K⁺ can fall fast once you start insulin), creatinine/eGFR (drives insulin clearance and metformin eligibility), bicarbonate and the anion gap (screening for occult DKA), and corrected Na⁺.Admit + daily
β-hydroxybutyrate (serum)Order it if: glucose >250–300 mg/dL and unwell; any anion-gap acidosis; type 1 diabetes with vomiting or missed insulin; any patient on an SGLT2 inhibitor who is ill, fasting, or post-operative — this is the only way to catch euglycemic DKA. Serum β-OHB beats urine ketones, which measure acetoacetate and can look falsely reassuring early and falsely persistent late.If indicated
Magnesium & phosphateIf glucose has been persistently high (osmotic diuresis wastes both), if refeeding is anticipated, or if K⁺ won't correct — hypomagnesemia causes refractory hypokalemia.If indicated
Infection workupUnexplained hyperglycemia is frequently the first sign of a new infection. If insulin requirements suddenly climb without a medication change, look for a source: urinalysis + culture, blood cultures, chest imaging, wound/foot exam.If unexplained
Nutrition / diet orderA consistent-carbohydrate diet (fixed grams per tray) — ADA 2026 notes this is preferred by most hospitals because it lets you match prandial insulin to a known carbohydrate load. Avoid "no concentrated sweets" and avoid "meals on demand" for insulin-treated patients (it uncouples the meal triad and causes insulin stacking).Admit
Nurse-initiated hypoglycemia protocolAttached to every insulin order — §16.12. The nurse must be able to treat a glucose <70 without paging first.Admit
Diabetes / glucose management team consult§16.3 (Grade B) — consult a specialized team when available. A virtual glucose management service reduced both hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia by 30–40%, and specialist teams shorten length of stay and cut 30-day readmissions.Strongly consider
Foot examOnce, on every diabetic inpatient — shoes and socks off. It takes 60 seconds and finds ulcers nobody mentioned.Admit

Imaging — what to order, when, and the threshold that triggers it

StudyTrigger to orderWhat you are looking for
Chest radiographFever, hypoxia, cough, or unexplained rise in insulin requirementPneumonia as the precipitant of hyperglycemia. Infection is the most common driver of a sudden loss of glycemic control.
Plain radiograph of the footAny diabetic foot ulcer at presentationGas in soft tissue, foreign body, and cortical destruction. Insensitive early — osteomyelitis needs ~2 weeks and 30–50% bone-mineral loss before X-ray changes appear, so a normal film does not exclude it.
MRI of the footUlcer with a positive probe-to-bone test, ulcer >2 cm², ulcer failing to heal, or ESR >70 mm/h with a normal X-rayThe reference standard for osteomyelitis: marrow oedema (low T1, high T2/STIR) with cortical destruction. Drives the choice between 2 weeks of antibiotics and 6 weeks ± resection.
CT abdomen/pelvis with contrastAbdominal pain with hyperglycemia; suspected intra-abdominal sourceEmphysematous cholecystitis/pyelonephritis, abscess, pancreatitis. Check eGFR and the metformin status before ordering (see the ACR rule in the Clinic panel).
Gastric ultrasound (point-of-care)Patient on a GLP-1 or GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonist going for a procedure under sedation or general anesthesiaResidual gastric contents despite adequate fasting. ADA 2026 lists this as an option within a personalized perioperative approach.
Head CTAltered mental status after a normal fingerstick glucoseNever before the glucose. Hypoglycemia is faster to test and faster to reverse.

Interpreting the labs — what moves, why, and what fools you

LabDirection & mechanismFalsely highFalsely low
POC capillary glucoseThe number you act on. Reflects capillary, not venous, glucose — runs slightly higher post-prandially.Poor peripheral perfusion (shock, pressors, hypothermia) concentrates the sample; severe anemia (less red cell mass to dilute plasma glucose); some maltose/icodextrin-containing products with older GDH-PQQ strips.Edema at the sample site (dilution); erythrocytosis/polycythemia; venous stasis. ADA 2026 lists perfusion abnormalities, edema, anemia, erythrocytosis and several common hospital medications as recognized error sources — if the result doesn't fit the patient, repeat it and send a lab glucose.
Serum potassiumInsulin drives K⁺ into cells via Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase. Expect it to fall as you treat. Osmotic diuresis also wastes total-body K⁺, so a "normal" K⁺ in a hyperglycemic patient often masks a large deficit.Hemolyzed specimen, fist clenching, extreme leukocytosis/thrombocytosis, acidosis shifting K⁺ out of cells.Insulin therapy, β-agonists, alkalosis, unrecognized hypomagnesemia driving renal wasting.
Serum sodiumHyperglycemia is osmotically active and pulls water into the vasculature → dilutional (translocational) hyponatremia. Correct before you diagnose anything: add 1.6 mEq/L to the measured Na⁺ for every 100 mg/dL of glucose above 100 (or 2.4 for glucose >400).—Severe hypertriglyceridemia or paraproteinemia (pseudohyponatremia, with indirect ion-selective electrodes).
Creatinine / eGFRRises with the osmotic-diuresis volume depletion. Falling eGFR means rising insulin half-life — reduce the dose before the low happens.Cimetidine, trimethoprim, cobicistat (block tubular secretion, no true GFR change); high muscle mass; creatine supplements.Low muscle mass, sarcopenia, cirrhosis, amputation — the eGFR overestimates true function in exactly the frail patients most at risk of hypoglycemia.
Bicarbonate / anion gapThe DKA screen. AG = Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻); normal 8–12.Hypoalbuminemia hides a gap — add 2.5 to the AG for every 1 g/dL that albumin is below 4.0. A "normal" gap of 11 in a patient with albumin 2.0 is really 16.—
β-hydroxybutyrateThe dominant ketone in DKA. ≥3.0 mmol/L meets ADA 2026 ketosis criteria.—Urine ketone dipsticks measure acetoacetate, not β-OHB. Early in DKA the ratio favours β-OHB, so urine ketones can be falsely mild; during recovery β-OHB converts to acetoacetate and urine ketones look worse while the patient improves. Use serum β-OHB.
Hemoglobin A1cGlycation of hemoglobin over the red cell lifespan (~90–120 days).Iron-deficiency anemia (older red cell population), uremia (carbamylation), splenectomy, some hemoglobin variants by assay.Recent transfusion, acute blood loss, hemolysis, erythropoietin use, advanced CKD, pregnancy, hemoglobinopathies — all shorten red cell survival. Suspect this in most hospitalized patients.
The point-of-care meter is the instrument of this entire discipline. ADA 2026 requires FDA-approved, hospital-calibrated systems and warns explicitly about perfusion, edema, anemia and drug interference.

Medtd1 — CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons: Diabetic Type 1 adult man with insulin pump and CGM sensor.jpg
The CGM 20/20 rule. To accept a CGM reading as valid for dosing, it must be within ±20% of the POC value when glucose is ≥70 mg/dL, or within ±20 mg/dL when glucose is <70 mg/dL. Cross-check at least once daily. No CGM is FDA-approved for inpatient use — POC confirms every dosing decision.
Concept

Sliding scale vs scheduled insulin

⚖️

The single most important teaching point on the wards

ADA 2026 §16.10 — Grade A
Correction insulin ("sliding scale") is a SUPPLEMENT, not a therapy.
A scheduled regimen has three separable components, and correction is only the third:
  • Basal — restrains hepatic glucose output between meals and overnight. Needed whether or not the patient eats.
  • Prandial (nutritional) — covers the carbohydrate actually delivered, whether by tray, tube, or TPN. Held when the carbohydrate stops.
  • Correction (supplemental) — a small, scaled top-up that fixes the residual error of the first two. It is proportional to the total daily dose, and it is added on top — never instead.
ADA 2026 §16.10 (Grade A): "For most individuals, sole use of a correction or supplemental insulin without basal insulin (formerly referred to as a sliding scale) in the inpatient setting is discouraged."

Why sliding-scale-alone loses — the mechanism, then the data

The mechanism is a control-theory failure. A scale only acts after a high glucose is measured, so it is always chasing a value that is already several hours old. It provides no basal component at all, so hepatic glucose output runs unopposed all night. And because doses are given q4–6h with rapid insulin that lasts 3–5 h, you get a sawtooth: a spike, an over-correction, a trough, and another spike. Patients spend the day oscillating around the target without ever sitting in it.

Figure 3 — The sawtooth is the signature of correction-only insulin. Without a basal component there is nothing holding the floor, so every dose is a rescue rather than a plan.

The evidence — three randomized trials, one answer

TrialDesignResult
RABBIT-2
Umpierrez, Diabetes Care 2007;30:2181–6		n=130 insulin-naive medical inpatients with T2DM. Glargine + glulisine (TDD 0.4 U/kg if BG 140–200; 0.5 U/kg if BG 201–400, split 50/50) vs sliding-scale regular insulin 4×/day.Target BG <140 reached in 66% vs 38%. Mean glucose 27 mg/dL lower with basal-bolus (166 vs 193 mg/dL, P<0.01). Despite escalating doses, 14% of the sliding-scale group never got below 240 mg/dL. No difference in hypoglycemia or length of stay.
RABBIT-2 Surgery
Umpierrez, Diabetes Care 2011;34:256–61		n=211 general-surgery patients with T2DM. Glargine + glulisine, TDD 0.5 U/kg (reduced to 0.3 U/kg if age ≥70 or creatinine ≥2.0 mg/dL) vs SSI 4×/day.Mean daily glucose 145±32 vs 172±47 mg/dL (P<0.01). Composite complications 8.6% with basal-bolus vs 24.3% with SSI (OR 3.39, 95% CI 1.50–7.65, P=0.003). Wound infection 2.9% vs 10.3% (P=0.05). Honest caveat: glucose <70 occurred in 23.1% vs 4.7% (P<0.001), though severe hypoglycemia <40 did not differ (P=0.057).
Basal Plus
Umpierrez, Diabetes Care 2013;36:2169–74		n=375 medical and surgical inpatients. Basal-bolus vs basal + correction only ("basal plus") vs SSI.Basal-plus was as good as full basal-bolus. Treatment failure (>2 consecutive BG >240 or mean daily BG >240): 0% vs 2% vs 19% (P<0.001). BG <70: 16% vs 13% vs 3% (P=0.02); no difference in severe hypoglycemia <40 (P=0.76).
When correction-only insulin IS acceptable
ADA 2026 and the Endocrine Society both leave a genuine, narrow window. Correction alone is reasonable when all of the following hold:
  • Type 2 diabetes only — never type 1, never pancreatogenic diabetes.
  • Non-critically ill, on the general ward.
  • Mild hyperglycemia or stress hyperglycemia with glucose staying <180 mg/dL (ADA 2026's stated exception), or previously diet-controlled / non-insulin-managed diabetes.
  • Short anticipated stay, reliable oral intake, and reliable q4–6h monitoring.
  • Endocrine Society Rec 10.1: in a patient without known diabetes, start with correction alone — but add scheduled insulin once BG is ≥180 mg/dL on ≥2 occasions in a day.
When scheduled basal-bolus is required: any type 1 diabetes (always basal + correction, even NPO); anyone already on insulin at home; admission glucose ≥180 persistently; A1c ≥ ~7.5–8%; on glucocorticoids; on continuous enteral feeds or TPN; anticipated stay >1–2 days with ongoing hyperglycemia; or correction-only has already failed for 24 hours.
In type 1 diabetes, correction-only insulin is contraindicated — full stop. ADA 2026 states it directly: dosing on premeal glucose alone accounts for neither basal requirement nor caloric intake, and increases both hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia. Basal insulin must never be held in type 1 diabetes, even when NPO, even when the glucose is normal — omission causes DKA within hours. Build an EHR alert if your hospital does not have one; ADA specifically recommends practice alerts to stop basal insulin being held during care transitions.
Treat

Building basal-bolus from scratch

🧮

Four steps, every time

insulin-naive patient

Step 1 — Estimate the total daily dose (TDD) from weight

ADA 2026 gives 0.3–0.6 units/kg/day as the usual starting range. Where you land inside that range is the clinical judgement, and it is driven by hypoglycemia risk on one side and insulin resistance on the other.

PatientStarting TDDWhy
Age ≥70, and/or eGFR <45, and/or creatinine ≥2.0 mg/dL, and/or on dialysis0.25–0.3 U/kg/dayReduced renal insulin clearance + reduced counterregulation + smaller muscle mass. This is the exact reduction rule used in RABBIT-2 Surgery (0.5 → 0.3 U/kg for age ≥70 or Cr ≥2.0).
Underweight, frail, poor or unpredictable oral intake0.25–0.3 U/kg/dayLess glucose entering, less muscle to store it, minimal reserve against a low.
Insulin-naive, BG 140–200 mg/dL0.4 U/kg/dayThe RABBIT-2 starting dose for this glucose band.
Insulin-naive, BG 201–400 mg/dL0.5 U/kg/dayThe RABBIT-2 starting dose for this glucose band; also the RABBIT-2 Surgery default.
Obese (BMI >30), markedly insulin resistant, or on glucocorticoids0.5–0.6 U/kg/day (occasionally higher)Receptor-level resistance means more insulin is needed for the same effect. Steroids alone typically raise requirements ~50%.
Type 1 diabetes, insulin-naive presentation~0.4 U/kg/day (often 0.3–0.5)Absolute deficiency, but no insulin resistance — they need replacement, not override. Get endocrine involved.

Starting range 0.3–0.6 U/kg/day per ADA Standards of Care 2026 §16; the glucose-banded 0.4 / 0.5 U/kg figures and the 0.3 U/kg reduction for age ≥70 or creatinine ≥2.0 mg/dL are the RABBIT-2 and RABBIT-2 Surgery protocols; the 0.25 U/kg lower tier for advanced CKD is from the AAFP inpatient glucose review. Round to a practical dose and re-check daily.

Do not exceed ~0.6 U/kg/day as a starting dose. Starting doses above 0.6–0.8 U/kg/day carry roughly three-fold higher odds of hypoglycemia. You can always titrate up tomorrow; you cannot un-give insulin. When you are genuinely unsure — start low.

Step 2 — Split it 50% basal / 50% nutritional

ADA 2026: "Half of the estimated total daily insulin should be given as basal insulin and half as nutritional insulin." Divide the nutritional half equally across the three meals.

TDD = weight × U/kg→ Basal = 50% of TDD, once daily (glargine)+ Prandial = 50% of TDD ÷ 3, with each meal (lispro/aspart)+ Correction scale on top, before each meal

Hold the prandial dose if the meal is not eaten. Write it as "hold if patient eats <50% of tray" or, better, give rapid-acting insulin immediately after the meal, dosed to what was actually consumed — an entirely legitimate strategy when intake is erratic, and far safer than pre-dosing a tray that goes untouched.

Step 3 — Add the correction (supplemental) scale

ADA 2026: correction scales should be proportional to the total daily dose — low scale for TDD <40 U/day, medium for 40–80 U/day, high for >80 U/day — and correction dosing should typically start at 140 or 150 mg/dL. Give correction with each pre-meal prandial dose, and every 4–6 h if the patient is not eating.

Representative scale reproduced from Endotext, "Inpatient Diabetes Management", consistent with the ADA 2026 principle that the scale be proportional to TDD. Use your institution's approved scale — they differ, and the nursing workflow is built around the local one.

The bedtime column matters more than the daytime columns. A full correction dose at 2200 with no food behind it is the classic set-up for the 0300 low — and remember that 78% of inpatient hypoglycemia occurs in patients on basal insulin, peaking between midnight and 6 AM. Use a reduced (or zero) bedtime scale and treat a bedtime glucose of 160 as fine.

These are starting estimates, not prescriptions — confirm against the actual glucose response. Endocrine Society Rec 9.1 advises against carbohydrate counting for prandial dosing in non-insulin-treated type 2 diabetes (Rec 9.2 permits either approach in insulin-treated patients), so in most ward patients fixed prandial dosing is the simpler and equally valid choice.

Worked example — do this one out loud on rounds

Mr. R is a 62-year-old man, 88 kg, BMI 31, admitted with cellulitis. He has type 2 diabetes on metformin 1000 mg BID at home, no insulin. Creatinine 1.0 (eGFR 78). Admission glucose 264 mg/dL, A1c 9.4%. He is eating full trays.

  1. Hold the metformin — he is acutely infected, and IV contrast may be needed.
  2. Choose the U/kg. BG is 201–400 → 0.5 U/kg/day (RABBIT-2). He is obese, which supports staying at 0.5 rather than dropping to 0.4. He is 62 with normal renal function, so no reduction. 0.5 U/kg/day.
  3. TDD = 88 kg × 0.5 = 44 units/day.
  4. Basal = 50% = 22 units. Glargine 22 units subcutaneously once daily at 2200.
  5. Prandial = 50% = 22 units ÷ 3 meals ≈ 7 units. Lispro 7 units subcutaneously with breakfast, lunch and dinner — hold if he eats less than half the tray.
  6. Correction: TDD is 44 U/day → 40–80 band → the usual scale, added to each pre-meal lispro dose, with the reduced bedtime column at 2200.
  7. Sanity-check with the rules: ISF = 1800 ÷ 44 ≈ 41 mg/dL per unit. So the "usual" scale giving 4 units at a glucose of 230 should drop him about 165 points, from 230 toward ~65 — too much. This is exactly why correction is layered on top of prandial insulin at a target of 150, not used to drive him to 100. It is also why you re-check and titrate rather than trusting the scale blindly.
  8. Orders also include: POC glucose before meals and at bedtime; A1c (already 9.4% — this predicts he will need insulin at discharge); consistent-carbohydrate diet; nurse-initiated hypoglycemia protocol.

Next morning: fasting glucose 208, pre-lunch 245, pre-dinner 230, bedtime 260. He is uniformly high, tolerating food, no hypoglycemia → increase the whole TDD by ~10–20%. New TDD ≈ 52 U → glargine 26 units, lispro 8–9 units per meal. Reassess again in 24 hours.

A starting point for an insulin-naive adult — always apply clinical judgement and your institution's protocol.

Convert

The patient already on home insulin

🔁

Continue, convert, and when to cut the dose

Endo Society Rec 10.3 — STRONG

This is the only strong recommendation in the entire Endocrine Society 2022 guideline: "Continue the scheduled insulin regimen, modified for nutritional status and severity of illness." Both halves matter. Continuing is not optional — stopping insulin in type 1 diabetes causes DKA, and stopping it in insulin-requiring type 2 diabetes causes runaway hyperglycemia. But continuing it unmodified is how you cause the 3 AM hypoglycemia.

The starting point

Home TDD× ~80% (ADA 2026 default)→ split 50% basal / 50% prandial→ apply further reductions below if any apply

ADA 2026 lists calculating the initial inpatient total daily dose as 80% of the home insulin dose as one of the accepted methods (alongside weight-based dosing, the prior hospitalization dose, and extrapolation from an infusion rate). The 20% haircut exists because hospital patients eat less, move less, and are frequently interrupted by procedures.

When to reduce further — and by how much

SituationAdjustmentMechanism
Reduced or unreliable oral intakeReduce TDD 20–25%; hold prandial doses entirely, or give post-meal based on what was eatenThe nutritional component has no substrate to cover. Basal continues.
NPOHold all prandial insulin. Continue basal at 50–80% of the usual dose. Correction q4–6hBasal covers hepatic output, which does not stop when the tray does. See the NPO module below for the specific per-insulin reductions.
New AKI or falling eGFRReduce TDD 20–25% now; further reduction (to ~50–75% of usual) if eGFR <30 or on dialysisRoughly 30–40% of insulin is cleared by the kidney; as eGFR falls, insulin half-life lengthens and effective dose rises without you changing anything. Kidney failure is an independent risk factor for inpatient hypoglycemia (ADA 2026).
Age ≥70, frail, low muscle massReduce 20–25% and target the upper half of the rangeBlunted counterregulation, less glycogen reserve, atypical hypoglycemia presentation (falls, confusion — not sweating).
Any inpatient hypoglycemia (<70)Reduce the responsible component 10–20% immediately — mandatory review under §16.1384% of severe lows were preceded by a milder low in the same admission. Reacting to the first one is what prevents the second.
Sepsis or shock resolving; vasopressors weaning; steroids taperingPre-emptively reduce 10–20% per step downInsulin resistance falls as fast as the illness does. The dose that was right yesterday is dangerous today.
Home regimen was a premixed insulin (70/30, 75/25)Convert to basal-bolus. Take the total daily premix units → give ~50% as basal, ~50% split across mealsADA 2026: premixes are not recommended in hospital — a fixed ratio cannot be unbundled when a meal is missed, and randomized data show more hypoglycemia.
Home regimen was U-500 regular insulinExpect the inpatient requirement to fall by up to 75%. Use a pen or pharmacy-drawn dose. Consult endocrineADA 2026 states this explicitly, and notes it happens regardless of pre-admission control. U-500 is a classic ten-fold error.
Home regimen was degludec or weekly icodecDo not stack a full new basal on topDegludec acts >40 h; icodec ≥7 days. Insulin given before admission is still working. Reduce early rather than trying to hold it off later.
Poor home adherence / not actually taking itDose as if insulin-naive (weight-based), not from the prescriptionADA 2026 explicitly says the decision to restart the home plan must account for the individual's actual adoption of it.

Insulin pumps and CGM: keep them running

ADA 2026 §16.7 (Grade C) says to continue insulin pump and automated insulin delivery use in hospital when clinically appropriate — contingent on supplies, staff training, competency assessment, and an institutional protocol. §16.6 (Grade B) says the same for personal CGM, with confirmatory POC glucose for every insulin dosing decision.

  • Requirements to continue a pump: the patient is alert, willing and physically able to self-manage; has their own supplies; agrees daily with the team that self-management remains appropriate; and there is a signed order plus documentation of settings (basal rates, ratios).
  • Stop the pump and convert to subcutaneous basal-bolus if: the patient is critically ill or hemodynamically unstable; obtunded, delirious or sedated; going for prolonged surgery or MRI; in DKA; unable to manage the device; or the hospital lacks pump expertise and the stay will exceed 1–2 days (Endo Society Rec 3.1).
  • Converting off a pump: total the 24-hour basal rates → that is the basal dose. Give the first long-acting basal dose 1–2 hours before disconnecting the pump (the pump's rapid insulin lasts only minutes once stopped). Then add prandial and correction as usual.
  • CGM and AID data should be reviewed and documented daily, with POC cross-check at least once a day using the 20/20 rule.
ADA notes fewer than half of surveyed hospitals have a diabetes-technology policy. If yours doesn't, the safe default is: continue the CGM as a trend monitor, dose only off POC values, and convert the pump to subcutaneous insulin if there is any doubt about the patient's ability to run it.
Special

Steroid-induced hyperglycemia

💥

Match the insulin curve to the steroid curve

the most predictable problem on the wards

Glucocorticoids are given to 10–15% of hospitalized patients and cause hyperglycemia in 56–86% of them, with or without preexisting diabetes (ADA 2026). Unlike almost everything else in this guide, it is entirely predictable — which means it should be anticipated, not discovered.

The signature pattern

Once-daily morning prednisone or prednisolone reaches peak plasma level at 4–6 h but exerts pharmacologic effect through the day. On CGM the pattern is unmistakable (ADA 2026): normal or only mildly elevated fasting glucose, a rise through the afternoon, and a peak in the evening, then a drift back toward baseline overnight. Reviews of glucocorticoid-induced hyperglycemia describe the rise beginning about 3–4 h after the dose and lasting 12–16 h.

This pattern is a trap for the unwary. A patient on morning prednisone can have a beautiful fasting glucose of 105 and a pre-dinner glucose of 320. If you only look at the morning number — or worse, if you escalate basal insulin to chase the evening numbers — you will produce overnight hypoglycemia while never touching the afternoon peak. Steroid hyperglycemia is a daytime problem and needs a daytime insulin.
Figure 4 — Why NPH is the steroid insulin. NPH's 4–6 h peak lands on the afternoon glucose rise and is gone by the time the steroid effect fades overnight.

Dosing — weight-based, indexed to the steroid dose

ADA 2026 recommends administering NPH concomitantly with prednisone/prednisolone, precisely because NPH peaks at 4–6 h. The Endocrine Society (Rec 2.1, conditional) accepts either an NPH-based or a basal-bolus approach. The published conversion table indexes the basal/NPH dose to the steroid dose:

Prednisone / prednisoloneDexamethasone equivalentNPH (or basal) doseTiming
≥40 mg/day≥8 mg/day0.4 U/kg/dayNPH with the morning steroid dose
30 mg/day6 mg/day0.3 U/kg/dayNPH with the morning steroid dose
20 mg/day4 mg/day0.2 U/kg/dayNPH with the morning steroid dose
10 mg/day2 mg/day0.1 U/kg/dayNPH with the morning steroid dose

Conversion table per the published review of glucocorticoid-induced hyperglycemia (Endocrinol Metab — "Glucocorticoid-Induced Hyperglycemia: A Neglected Problem"), consistent with ADA 2026 §16's NPH-with-steroid strategy. This is added to any existing basal-bolus regimen or oral agents, not instead of them.

ScenarioWhat to giveWhy
Once- or twice-daily prednisone / prednisolone / methylprednisoloneNPH given at the same time as the steroid, dosed per the table. If the steroid is BID, split the NPH BID to match.NPH's 4–6 h peak mirrors the steroid's glucose curve and fades overnight when the steroid effect fades.
Dexamethasone, or continuous/multi-dose steroidsLong-acting basal insulin (glargine/detemir), increased as needed — NPH's peak is wasted against a flat, 36–72 h steroid effect.ADA 2026: for long-acting glucocorticoids and multi-dose/continuous use, long-acting basal insulin may be required to manage fasting glucose.
High steroid doses, patient eatingIncrease prandial and correction insulin — ADA 2026 says sometimes as much as 40–60% or more — in addition to basal.The dominant defect is post-prandial: steroids block peripheral glucose disposal. Some protocols shift the split toward ~65–70% prandial / 30–35% basal.
Patient already on basal-bolus who is starting steroidsAnticipate a ~50% rise in total requirement; add the NPH per the table, or increase the existing TDD, and check glucose more frequently for 48 h.Do not wait for a glucose of 400 to react — the rise is predictable.
Steroid is being TAPERED or STOPPEDReduce insulin at the same time, by roughly the same proportion. If the steroid stops abruptly, cut or stop the steroid-directed NPH that same day.ADA 2026 lists "a sudden reduction of corticosteroid dose" as a leading cause of iatrogenic inpatient hypoglycemia. This is the most common serious steroid-insulin error — the steroid comes off and the insulin doesn't.
Worked example — steroid add-on

Ms. K, 70 kg, admitted with a COPD exacerbation, started on prednisone 40 mg daily at 8 AM. Known type 2 diabetes, home metformin only (held). Fasting glucose 118, pre-lunch 214, pre-dinner 336, bedtime 290.

The pattern is diagnostic: normal fasting, escalating through the day, peaking at dinner — textbook morning-prednisone hyperglycemia. Increasing basal insulin here would fix nothing and cause a 3 AM low.

  • Prednisone 40 mg → NPH 0.4 U/kg = 70 × 0.4 = 28 units of NPH, given at 8 AM with the prednisone.
  • Add a correction scale before meals (she is insulin-resistant on steroids → use the resistant column) with the reduced bedtime column.
  • Because she is eating and the defect is post-prandial, add prandial lispro if the daytime numbers stay above target after 24 h.
  • When prednisone drops to 20 mg → NPH falls to 0.2 U/kg = 14 units, same day. When prednisone stops → stop the NPH entirely and reassess; she may need nothing beyond her home metformin.
