Special

NPO, tube feeds & TPN

🍽️

When the carbohydrate changes, the insulin must change with it

The universal rule. Hold the prandial insulin when the nutrition stops. Continue the basal (usually reduced). Keep giving correction every 4–6 hours. Never do the reverse — the single most dangerous inpatient insulin order is "hold all insulin, NPO," because in type 1 diabetes that produces DKA and in anyone it produces uncontrolled hyperglycemia.

NPO for a procedure or surgery

InsulinAdjustment the night before / morning ofSource
Long-acting basal analog (glargine, detemir) — evening doseGive 75–80% of the usual dose (i.e. reduce by ~20–25%)ADA 2026: a 25% reduction of basal the evening before surgery is more likely to achieve perioperative goals with lower hypoglycemia risk
Long-acting basal analog — morning doseGive 75–80% of the usual doseADA 2026 §16 perioperative section
NPHGive one-half of the usual doseADA 2026 explicitly specifies NPH to one-half
Prandial / nutritional insulinHOLD entirely while NPONo carbohydrate to cover
Correction insulinContinue q4–6h (rapid-acting q4h, or regular q6h)ADA 2026
Non-insulin agentsHold metformin and all oral agents on the day of surgery. SGLT2 inhibitor held 3–4 days prior. GLP-1 RA per the personalized approachADA 2026: "Insulin is the only recommended glucose-lowering medication in the perioperative period"
Insulin pumpMay continue during surgery if institutional policy allows; otherwise convert to an insulin infusion or basal + correction before the caseADA 2026 §16

Monitoring while NPO: check glucose every 2–4 h perioperatively (ADA 2026), or every 4–6 h on the ward. Target 100–180 mg/dL before, during and after surgery (§16.15). Consider a D5 or D10 infusion in patients receiving basal insulin who will be NPO for a prolonged period, especially in type 1 diabetes.

ADA 2026 also advises against carbohydrate-containing oral fluids preoperatively in patients with diabetes (Endo Society Rec 8.1) — the "carbohydrate loading" ERAS protocols used in non-diabetic surgical patients do not apply here.

Continuous enteral tube feeds

A continuous feed creates a continuous post-prandial state. This changes both the insulin choice and the target.

ComponentDoseNotes
BasalContinue the usual basal (or ~50% of estimated TDD)ADA 2026: most adults receiving basal insulin should continue their basal dose. Never cover the whole requirement with basal alone — that is what makes a feed interruption catastrophic.
Nutritional1 unit of insulin per 10–15 g of carbohydrate in the formulaADA 2026. Practical alternative: nutritional dose ≈ estimated TDD ÷ 10, given every 4 h.
Delivery optionsRegular insulin q6h (preferred), rapid-acting q4h, or NPH q8–12hADA 2026 notes a regular-insulin-based plan achieved better glycemic management with fewer daily injections in patients on continuous feeds — regular's 6–8 h duration matches the continuous carbohydrate delivery better than a 3–5 h analog.
CorrectionSubcutaneous regular q6h or rapid-acting q4hMatch the correction interval to the correction insulin's duration to avoid stacking.
TargetDo not aim below 140 mg/dLADA 2026: efforts to bring glucose below 140 in patients on continuous nutrition "substantially increase the risk of hypoglycemia."
If the feed is interruptedStart IV dextrose (D10) for the duration of the active insulin, and check glucose q1–2hADA 2026. Write this as a standing order when you start the feed, not after the first hypoglycemic event. Nurses hold feeds for imaging, repositioning, high residuals and tube displacement all the time.

Bolus and nocturnal enteral feeds

  • Bolus feeds: give approximately 1 unit of rapid-acting insulin per 10–15 g of carbohydrate subcutaneously before each bolus, plus correction insulin as needed before each feeding (ADA 2026).
  • Nocturnal feeds: give NPH at the time the feed is started to cover the overnight nutritional load — its 4–12 h action profile matches an 8–12 h nocturnal feed. This is a specifically recommended approach in ADA 2026.

Total parenteral nutrition

  • Put the insulin in the bag. For continuous peripheral or central TPN, add human regular insulin to the TPN solution, particularly if more than 20 units of correction insulin have been needed in the past 24 hours.
  • Starting dose: 1 unit of regular insulin per 10 g of dextrose in the bag (ADA 2026), adjusted daily. An equivalent way to express the same thing is ~0.1 unit per gram of dextrose.
  • Why in the bag? ADA 2026 states this is the safest way to prevent hypoglycemia if the TPN is stopped or interrupted — the insulin stops at exactly the same instant as the glucose. Subcutaneous glargine achieves equivalent control but does not have this safety property.
  • Correction insulin is still given subcutaneously on top, q4–6h.
Worked example — continuous tube feeds

Mr. T, 75 kg, post-stroke, on continuous enteral feeds delivering 150 g of carbohydrate per 24 h. Type 2 diabetes; glucose running 230–290 mg/dL.

  • Estimate TDD: 75 kg × 0.4 U/kg = 30 units/day (he is not obese and not on steroids).
  • Basal: 50% = glargine 15 units daily.
  • Nutritional: 150 g carbohydrate ÷ 12 g per unit ≈ 12–15 units/day — cross-checks nicely with TDD ÷ 2. Give as regular insulin 3 units subcutaneously every 6 hours (4 doses = 12 units), which ADA 2026 favours over q4h analog dosing for continuous feeds.
  • Correction: regular insulin q6h using the sensitive-to-usual scale, given at the same times as the scheduled regular.
  • Target 140–180, not 100–180 — he is continuously post-prandial.
  • Standing order written at the same time: "If enteral feeds are held for any reason, start D10 at the current feed rate and check glucose q1–2h until feeds resume or scheduled insulin has worn off."
Safety

Hypoglycemia — recognize, treat, then fix the regimen

🚨

The protocol, and the step everyone skips

ADA 2026 §16.12 / §16.13
LevelGlucoseMeaning
Level 154–69 mg/dL
(3.0–3.8 mmol/L)		Alert value. Treat promptly to prevent progression — ADA 2026 is explicit that prompt treatment of level 1 prevents level 2 and 3.
Level 2<54 mg/dL
(<3.0 mmol/L)		Clinically significant — typically the threshold for neuroglycopenic symptoms. Requires immediate intervention.
Level 3Severe — any glucoseA clinical event with altered mental and/or physical functioning requiring assistance from another person. Defined by the clinical state, not a number.

Treatment — the 15-15 rule and its alternatives

1
Awake, alert, able to swallow, NOT NPO
The 15-15 rule
▾

Give 15 grams of fast-acting carbohydrate, recheck the glucose in 15 minutes, and repeat until glucose is stable above 70 mg/dL (ADA 2026). Some inpatient protocols use 20 g.

What counts as 15 g: 4 glucose tablets · 4 oz (½ cup) of juice or regular soda · 1 tablespoon of honey or sugar · 8 oz of milk (slower — contains fat and protein). What does not count: anything sugar-free or "diet"; chocolate, cookies or ice cream (fat delays absorption); and orange juice given to a patient with hyperkalemia concerns.

Then give a snack or meal containing protein and complex carbohydrate if the next meal is more than an hour away — 15 g of glucose lasts about 30–45 minutes, and the insulin that caused the low is still working.

2
Unable to swallow, NPO, or obtunded — WITH IV access
IV dextrose
▾

D50W: 25 grams = 50 mL of 50% dextrose IV push. Many protocols use half an amp (12.5 g / 25 mL) first for milder lows to avoid a rebound spike. Recheck glucose every 15 minutes and repeat until glucose is stable (many inpatient protocols target ≥100 mg/dL before stopping).

D10W is a reasonable alternative — 25 g in 250 mL, infused until the patient responds. Studies suggest D10 is as effective as D50 for resolving hypoglycemia with less rebound hyperglycemia and less risk of extravasation injury (D50 is hyperosmolar and sclerosing — give it through a well-running, large IV, never a small hand vein if avoidable).

Then start a continuous D5W or D10W infusion if the cause is long-acting — a sulfonylurea, a large basal insulin dose, or renal failure. One amp of D50 will not hold a glyburide overdose.

3
No IV access, or IV access will be delayed
Glucagon
▾

Glucagon 1 mg intramuscularly or subcutaneously (adults and children >25 kg); may also be given IV. If there is no response after 15 minutes, a second 1 mg dose may be given from a new kit. Nasal glucagon is 3 mg as one spray into one nostril, repeatable once from a new device.

Glucagon works by mobilizing hepatic glycogen — so it fails, or works poorly, in exactly the patients most likely to need it: starvation, prolonged fasting, alcohol use, cirrhosis or advanced liver disease, adrenal insufficiency, and glycogen storage disease. It also does not help in sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia (it stimulates further insulin release). Expect vomiting — protect the airway.

Get IV access and give dextrose as soon as you can. Glucagon is a bridge, not a treatment.

A glucagon rescue kit. Every patient discharged on insulin or a sulfonylurea should leave with one — and someone at home should know how to use it.
MallardTV — CC0 · Wikimedia Commons: Glucagon 1.jpg
Subcutaneous injection technique. Site matters: abdominal absorption is fastest and most consistent; a lipohypertrophic site absorbs erratically and is a common hidden cause of unexplained glucose swings — examine the injection sites.
British Columbia Institute of Technology — CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons: Subcutaneous injection with insulin needle.jpg
The step everyone skips: change the regimen.
ADA 2026 §16.13 (Grade C) requires that the treatment plan be reviewed and changed whenever a glucose <70 mg/dL is documented. This is not paperwork. The data behind it:
  • 84% of inpatients with severe hypoglycemia (<40 mg/dL) had an earlier episode <70 mg/dL during the same admission.
  • 78% of episodes <50 mg/dL occurred in patients on basal insulin, and incidence peaked between midnight and 6 AM.
  • Yet 75% of those patients had no change made to the basal dose before the next dose was given.
Treating the low and walking away is how the next, worse low happens.

What to change, based on when the low occurred

Timing of the lowCulpritAction
Fasting / overnight / 0300Excess basal insulin (or a bedtime correction dose given with no food behind it)Reduce basal by 10–20%. Remove or reduce the bedtime correction column. Remember: a fasting glucose <100 predicts a low in the next 24 h — reduce basal before it happens.
Before lunchExcess breakfast prandial dose, or breakfast not eatenReduce the breakfast prandial dose by 10–20%, or convert to post-meal dosing based on intake.
Before dinnerExcess lunch prandial dose; or NPH given in the morning peaking in the late afternoonReduce the lunch dose, or reduce the morning NPH.
Any time, after a steroid taperInsulin not reduced with the steroidCut the steroid-directed insulin proportionally, same day. ADA lists abrupt steroid reduction as a leading cause of iatrogenic hypoglycemia.
Any time, after feeds/TPN stoppedNutritional insulin still on board with no substrateStart D10, hold the nutritional insulin, and write the standing interruption order.
Any time, with a rising creatinineFalling insulin clearanceReduce TDD 20–25%; more if eGFR <30.
Recurrent, unexplainedConsider: adrenal insufficiency, sepsis, liver failure, malnutrition, insulin errors, a sulfonylurea nobody stopped, or factitious/medication errorEscalate — check a cortisol, review the MAR line by line, and involve the diabetes team.

Other ADA-listed precipitants of iatrogenic inpatient hypoglycemia worth memorizing: reduced oral intake, emesis, mistimed rapid-acting insulin relative to meals, reduced IV dextrose infusion rate, unexpected interruption of enteral or parenteral feeding, prolonged procedures, delayed or missed glucose checks, and an altered ability to report symptoms. Bundled prevention programs reduced inpatient hypoglycemia by 56–80%.

Monitor

Daily titration — reading the fingerstick pattern

📈

Adjust once a day, using the pattern — not the last number

Every morning, lay out the last 24 hours of glucose values in order and ask which component is failing. The pattern names the culprit.

Pattern over 24 hWhat it meansChange
Fasting high, rest of day acceptableInsufficient basalIncrease basal 10–20%. A useful rule of thumb graded by the fasting value: FBG 141–160 → +2–3 U; 161–180 → +4–5 U; 181–200 → +6–7 U; >200 → +8 U.
Fasting fine, post-meal / pre-next-meal highInsufficient prandial insulinIncrease the prandial dose for the preceding meal by 10–20% (or 1–2 units). Do not increase basal — that is over-basalization and causes nocturnal lows.
High at every single checkWhole regimen underdosedIncrease total TDD by 10–20% and redistribute 50/50. Also look for a new precipitant: infection, new steroid, new pressor, a hidden dextrose infusion.
Only the pre-dinner value high, on morning steroidsSteroid effect — classic afternoon peakAdd or increase morning NPH, and/or increase lunch prandial and correction. Do not chase it with basal.
Correction insulin needed at almost every checkThe scheduled doses are too low — correction is doing the scheduled insulin's jobAdd roughly the total correction units used in the last 24 h into tomorrow's scheduled doses, split between basal and prandial according to when they were needed. This is the single most useful daily-titration move.
Any value <70Excess insulin somewhereReduce the responsible component 10–20% before the next dose. Mandatory under §16.13.
Fasting <100 with no symptomatic low yetImpending hypoglycemiaReduce basal 10–20% now — ADA 2026 states this value "necessitates basal insulin dose adjustments."
Wildly erratic, no patternProcess failure, not physiologyCheck the meal triad: is the glucose being checked, the tray delivered, and the insulin given within a coordinated window? Also check injection sites for lipohypertrophy, verify the insulin type on the MAR, and confirm doses were actually administered rather than "held."

The graded fasting-glucose basal titration increments above are a representative inpatient protocol (Endotext, Inpatient Diabetes Management); ADA 2026 does not mandate specific increments but calls for daily adjustment guided by glycemia and anticipated changes in nutrition and medications. The RABBIT-2 protocol adjusted the total daily dose by ±20% per day based on response.

Change one thing a day, and write down why. Insulin has a ~24-hour feedback loop; if you change basal and prandial and the correction scale simultaneously, you learn nothing from tomorrow's numbers. The exception is a hypoglycemic event, where you act immediately.
Context

Comorbidity interactions

🔗

How each comorbidity changes the course and the management

ComorbidityHow it changes the courseHow it changes management
CKD stage 4–5 / ESRD on dialysisInsulin half-life rises as renal clearance falls; hypoglycemia risk climbs sharply and is independently associated with kidney failure (ADA 2026). Glucose also shifts around dialysis sessions.Reduce TDD 25–50%. Relax targets toward 140–180 (up to 200–250 in advanced failure). Stop metformin at eGFR <30. Avoid glyburide entirely. Expect glucose to fall during hemodialysis (glucose-free dialysate) and to rise with glucose-containing peritoneal dialysate. Linagliptin is the DPP-4 inhibitor that needs no dose adjustment.
Cirrhosis / acute liver failureTwo opposing problems: hepatic insulin resistance causes hyperglycemia, while depleted glycogen stores cause profound, prolonged hypoglycemia that recovers poorly.Lower TDD, avoid long-acting sulfonylureas, and be aware that glucagon may fail (no glycogen to mobilize) — use IV dextrose, and often a continuous infusion. Watch for hypoglycemia with any reduction in oral intake.
Heart failureCongestion worsens insulin resistance; diabetes worsens HF outcomes. Diuresis and fluid shifts change glucose.ADA 2026 §16.11 (Grade A): initiate or continue an SGLT2 inhibitor if indicated for heart failure, absent contraindications, after recovery from the acute illness — and proactively adjust insulin and diuretic dosing. Avoid thiazolidinediones (fluid retention). Consider stopping saxagliptin/alogliptin (FDA advice in HF).
Sepsis / critical illnessMaximal counterregulatory surge and cytokine-driven insulin resistance — requirements can double, then halve within hours as the illness resolves or pressors wean.Move to an IV insulin infusion if requirements are high or changing fast (see the ICU panel). Anticipate a steep fall in requirement during recovery — the classic setting for ICU hypoglycemia.
Obesity / severe insulin resistanceHigher requirement per kg; injection into adipose tissue may absorb more slowly and variably.Start at the top of the range (0.5–0.6 U/kg/day) and use the resistant correction scale. Requirements of 1–2 U/kg/day are not unusual in established insulin-resistant type 2 diabetes.
Age ≥70 / frailty / dementiaBlunted counterregulation, reduced glycogen, atypical hypoglycemia (falls, confusion, not sweating), unpredictable intake.Start at 0.25–0.3 U/kg/day. Simplify the regimen wherever possible — fewer injections, no complex correction scales. Target the upper half of the range.
Solid organ transplantTacrolimus (> cyclosporine) is directly β-cell toxic; steroids compound it. Post-transplant diabetes is common and often permanent.Expect high, changing requirements. Insulin is the treatment of choice early. Coordinate with transplant — glucose improves as tacrolimus levels and steroid doses fall.
Active malignancy / palliative goalsOften on high-dose steroids, poor intake, cachexia — swinging between hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia.Relax targets substantially (up to 250 mg/dL). Reduce the frequency of fingersticks. In true comfort-focused care, consider stopping glucose monitoring and correction insulin entirely — but never stop basal insulin in type 1 diabetes, as DKA is a distressing way to die.
Adrenal insufficiencyCortisol deficiency removes a key counterregulatory hormone → recurrent, unexplained hypoglycemia.Consider it in any inpatient with recurrent unexplained lows, especially after steroid withdrawal. Check a morning cortisol; treat with stress-dose hydrocortisone — which will then raise the glucose and require insulin adjustment.
Pancreatogenic (type 3c) diabetes
post-pancreatectomy, chronic pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis		Both insulin and glucagon are deficient, so hypoglycemia is severe, prolonged, and poorly counterregulated. Exocrine insufficiency makes absorption erratic.Treat like brittle type 1 diabetes: always basal + correction, never sliding scale alone, low thresholds for endocrine consultation, and pancreatic enzyme replacement with meals.
PregnancyProgressive insulin resistance through gestation, then an abrupt fall postpartum; much tighter targets; DKA occurs at lower glucose levels.Out of scope here — involve maternal-fetal medicine and endocrinology. Cut insulin sharply immediately postpartum.
Alcohol use disorderEthanol inhibits gluconeogenesis and depletes glycogen → hypoglycemia, often overnight and often severe.Give thiamine before glucose. Anticipate hypoglycemia during withdrawal and with poor intake; glucagon works poorly.
Escalate

When to call the ICU

⬆️

Numeric thresholds for transfer or an insulin drip

Escalate to an IV insulin infusion and/or higher level of care when:
  • Persistent glucose >300–350 mg/dL (a widely used practice trigger, not a specific guideline threshold) despite two consecutive days of appropriately escalated subcutaneous basal-bolus insulin, or a total requirement climbing past ~1.5–2 U/kg/day.
  • DKA — glucose ≥200 mg/dL (or known diabetes) plus β-hydroxybutyrate ≥3.0 mmol/L or urine ketones ≥2+ plus pH <7.3 and/or bicarbonate <18 mmol/L (all three criteria required, ADA 2026 Table 16.1). Moderate/severe DKA belongs in the ICU or a step-down unit.
  • HHS — glucose ≥600 mg/dL, effective osmolality >300 mOsm/kg, β-OHB <3.0 mmol/L, pH ≥7.3 and bicarbonate ≥15 mmol/L. Usually with altered cognition; almost always ICU.
  • Shock, or any vasopressor requirement — subcutaneous absorption is unreliable when peripheral perfusion fails, so subcutaneous insulin becomes both ineffective and unpredictable (and may all absorb at once when perfusion is restored).
  • Post-cardiac-surgery hyperglycemia, or major surgery with persistent glucose >180 mg/dL.
  • Recurrent or refractory hypoglycemia requiring repeated dextrose — particularly a sulfonylurea overdose or a massive insulin dose, which needs a continuous dextrose infusion and hourly monitoring.
  • Level 3 hypoglycemia with seizure, coma, or airway compromise.
  • Severe hyperkalemia or profound electrolyte derangement requiring continuous cardiac monitoring alongside insulin therapy.
Do not "wait and see" on a widening anion gap. A ward patient whose bicarbonate is falling and anion gap widening is developing DKA regardless of what the glucose reads — and if they are on an SGLT2 inhibitor, the glucose may look entirely normal. Check β-hydroxybutyrate, start fluids, and escalate.
Dispo

Discharge readiness & disposition

🏠

Ready to go — and where to

Glycemic discharge readiness:

  • Glucose values predominantly 100–180 mg/dL for at least 24 hours on the regimen they are actually going home on — not on a hospital regimen you intend to change at the door.
  • No hypoglycemia (<70 mg/dL) in the preceding 24 hours.
  • Eating reliably, on the diet they will eat at home.
  • Held agents addressed: metformin restarted (creatinine at baseline, ≥48 h post-contrast if held for that), or a documented plan and date for restarting.
  • The acute precipitant treated — infection controlled, steroids at a stable dose with a written taper and a matching insulin taper.
  • Patient or caregiver can demonstrate: drawing/dialing the dose, injecting, checking a glucose, and stating what they will do for a glucose below 70.
  • Prescriptions written for insulin and needles, meter/strips or sensors, and glucagon; costs confirmed as affordable.
  • Follow-up booked — within 1 month, or 1–2 weeks if medications changed or control is not optimal (ADA 2026).
Not yet ready if: any hypoglycemia in the last 24 h; still on a steroid taper without a written matching insulin plan; the regimen was changed today and has not been observed for a full day; nobody at home can give injections and no home nursing is arranged; or the patient cannot afford the insulin you prescribed.

Home

Independent or has a capable caregiver; can self-inject and self-monitor; regimen is simple enough to execute; supplies and follow-up secured.

Home health

Needs nursing visits for insulin administration or teaching — common for newly insulin-requiring patients living alone, or after a new diagnosis. Simplify to once-daily basal if a nurse visits once daily.

SNF

Needs 24-hour skilled nursing (wound care, IV antibiotics, complex insulin) with <3 h/day of therapy. ADA 2026 §16.18 (new): confirm the facility can actually deliver the regimen — many cannot do QID checks or multi-tier correction scales. Simplify before transfer.

Acute rehab (IRF)

Can tolerate ≥3 h/day of therapy across ≥2 disciplines — e.g. post-stroke or post-amputation. Expect insulin requirements to fall as activity increases; reduce pre-emptively.

LTAC

Prolonged complex care >25 days — ventilator weaning, complex wounds, prolonged TPN. Insulin plans here are usually feed-linked; write explicit feed-interruption orders.

Hospice / palliative

Comfort-focused. Relax targets to symptom avoidance only; consider stopping fingersticks and correction insulin. Continue basal insulin in type 1 diabetes to prevent DKA.
🫀 ICU — intravenous insulin infusion & critical-care glycemic targets
Admit

Who needs an insulin drip

🚨

Indications & the ICU target

ADA 2026 §16.8a — Grade A
Start insulin at
≥180 mg/dL
confirmed ×2 within 24 h · §16.4a (A)
ICU target range
140–180 mg/dL
7.8–10.0 mmol/L · §16.5a (A)
More stringent, selected patients

e.g. post-cardiac surgery — only if achievable without significant hypoglycemia
Never target
80–110 mg/dL
NICE-SUGAR: higher mortality, 13× severe hypoglycemia

ADA 2026 §16.8a (Grade A): continuous intravenous insulin infusion is recommended for achieving glycemic goals and avoiding hypoglycemia in critically ill individuals. It is the most effective method in the critical care setting because the half-life of IV insulin is minutes, so the dose can be matched to a requirement that is changing hour by hour.

Practical indications: critical illness with persistent glucose ≥180 mg/dL · DKA and HHS · shock or any vasopressor requirement (subcutaneous absorption is unreliable when peripheral perfusion fails) · post-cardiac surgery · extensive burns · organ transplantation · high-dose steroids with refractory hyperglycemia · ward hyperglycemia refractory to escalated subcutaneous insulin · NPO with severe insulin resistance.

The ICU setting: multiple simultaneous infusions, changing pressor doses, interrupted nutrition. Every one of these changes the insulin requirement, which is exactly why a titratable IV infusion beats subcutaneous dosing here.
Pittigrilli — CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons: Patient lying in bed in intensive care unit…
A volumetric infusion pump. The standard insulin infusion is 1 unit of regular human insulin per mL of 0.9% NaCl — the 1:1 concentration is what makes bedside rate calculations survivable.
Orderinchaos — CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons: Baxter Colleague 3 CXE 1 at Joondalup 2020.jpg

Why the target is 140–180 and not 80–110 — the trial arc

This is one of the great reversals in critical care, and it is worth knowing the sequence because the reasoning recurs across ICU medicine.

TrialDesignResultWhat it changed
Leuven-1
Van den Berghe, NEJM 2001;345:1359–67		n=1,548 surgical ICU patients on mechanical ventilation. Intensive 80–110 mg/dL vs conventional (insulin only if >215; maintain 180–200).ICU mortality 4.6% vs 8.0% (P<0.04); among those in ICU >5 days, 10.6% vs 20.2% (P=0.005). In-hospital mortality ↓34%, bloodstream infections ↓46%, AKI requiring dialysis ↓41%, critical-illness polyneuropathy ↓44%.Launched a decade of tight glycemic control worldwide.
Leuven-2
Van den Berghe, NEJM 2006;354:449–61		n=1,200 medical ICU patients, same targets.In-hospital mortality 37.3% vs 40.0% — not significant (P=0.33). Morbidity did improve (less new kidney injury, faster weaning, earlier discharge). But among those in ICU <3 days, mortality was higher with intensive control; benefit appeared only at ≥3 days (52.5% → 43.0%, P=0.009) — a subgroup you cannot identify on admission.First serious crack: the benefit did not generalize from surgical to medical patients.
NICE-SUGAR
NEJM 2009;360:1283–97		n=6,104 medical and surgical ICU patients, international. Intensive 81–108 mg/dL vs conventional ≤180 mg/dL. Primary endpoint 90-day mortality.Intensive control increased mortality: 27.5% vs 24.9% (OR 1.14, 95% CI 1.02–1.28, P=0.02). Severe hypoglycemia (≤40 mg/dL) 6.8% vs 0.5% (P<0.001) — a roughly 13-fold increase. No difference in ICU/hospital days, ventilator days, or dialysis.Definitive. Ended tight glycemic control and set today's 140–180 target.
GLUCO-CABG
Umpierrez, Diabetes Care 2015;38:1665–72		n=302 post-CABG. Intensive 100–140 vs conservative 141–180 mg/dL.Mean ICU glucose 132±14 vs 154±17. Composite complications 42% vs 52%, not significant (P=0.08). Heterogeneity by diabetes status: no difference in patients with diabetes (49% vs 48%, P=0.87), but fewer complications with intensive control in patients without diabetes (34% vs 55%, P=0.008).Explains why §16.5a permits 110–140 in selected cardiac-surgery patients while keeping 140–180 as the default.
The unifying lesson: the harm of hypoglycemia is immediate and the benefit of near-normoglycemia is marginal, so the risk-benefit curve is asymmetric. ADA 2026 also cites a more recent multicenter trial in patients not receiving early parenteral nutrition that found no benefit of tight control despite excellent glucose separation and very low hypoglycemia in both arms (1.0% vs 0.7%) — reinforcing that the earlier Leuven benefit was probably specific to a nutrition strategy no longer used.
Monitor

Monitoring, access & the drip setup

🩸

Getting the infusion right before you start it

Concentration

ADA 2026; hourly until stable is typical

Potassium

fingersticks unreliable on pressors
Prime the tubing — this is not optional pharmacy trivia. Insulin adsorbs onto PVC tubing. Without priming, only about 84% of the intended dose actually reaches the patient; after a 10 mL flush the loss is still 6.6%; after a 20 mL flush the loss falls to 3.4% and priming further adds nothing. A patient who is "not responding to the drip" in the first hour may simply be receiving 84% of what you ordered.
Point-of-care fingersticks are least reliable in exactly the patient you are titrating. ADA 2026 lists perfusion abnormalities, edema, anemia and erythrocytosis as recognized sources of POC error — all common in shock. On vasopressors, use arterial or venous blood for glucose, not a fingerstick, and confirm any value that does not fit the clinical picture. CGM should not be used alone for glucose monitoring during surgery (§16), and no CGM is FDA-approved for inpatient use — although ADA notes hybrid protocols using CGM alongside periodic POC have successfully reduced the burden of hourly testing during IV titration.

What to trend in the unit

GlucoseHourly while titrating; may extend to q2h once three consecutive values are in range and the patient is otherwise stable; ADA permits q30 min–2 h depending on protocol and stability.Continuous
Potassium, magnesium, phosphateEvery 2–4 h initially. Insulin shifts K⁺ into cells; combined with osmotic losses this can drop K⁺ fast. Replete before it becomes an arrhythmia.q2–4h
Anion gap & β-hydroxybutyrateIf DKA is present or suspected, or if the patient is on an SGLT2 inhibitor. Resolution of DKA is defined by pH >7.3 or bicarbonate >18 mmol/L and ketones <0.6 mmol/L — not by the glucose.If indicated
Insulin infusion rate itselfTrend it like a vital sign. A rate that is climbing signals worsening illness or a new steroid; a rate that is falling predicts the transition and warns of impending hypoglycemia.Continuous
Nutrition statusNote every change in tube feeds, TPN and dextrose-containing infusions. An interrupted feed with an unchanged drip rate is the commonest ICU hypoglycemia mechanism.Continuous
Protocol

Running the infusion

💧

Initiation, titration, and what to do when it drops

Use your institution's validated protocol. ADA 2026 requires that infusions be "administered using validated written or computerized protocols that allow for predefined adjustments in the insulin infusion rate based on glycemic fluctuations and immediate past and current insulin infusion rates." That last clause is the key design principle: a good protocol titrates on both the current glucose and its rate of change, not on the glucose alone. The examples below illustrate the common architectures — the numbers differ between protocols and the local one governs.

Initiation — three common architectures

ProtocolTargetInitiation rule
Yale Insulin Infusion Protocol
Goldberg, Diabetes Care 2004;27:461		original 100–139 mg/dL
updated to 120–160 mg/dL in 2012		Initial BG 181–299 mg/dL: divide the glucose by 100 and round → that is the initial rate in units/h; no bolus.
Initial BG >300 mg/dL: divide by 100 and round → give that number as an IV bolus AND start that rate.
Example: BG 260 → start at 2.6 ≈ 2.5–3 units/h, no bolus. BG 420 → bolus ~4 units and start ~4 units/h.
Multiplier / nurse-managed protocol
e.g. Johns Hopkins		140–180 mg/dLInitial bolus and infusion rate = initial BG ÷ 200, rounded to the nearest 0.5 units. The divisor is 200, not 100, precisely because the target is the looser 140–180.
Ongoing: units/h = multiplier × (BG − 60), starting multiplier 0.02, raised or lowered as the glucose runs above or below target.
Weight-basedvariesCommonly 0.02–0.1 units/kg/h. For DKA/HHS specifically, ADA 2026 Figure 16.1 specifies 0.1 units/kg/h as a fixed-rate infusion (consider a 0.1 units/kg IV bolus if there is a delay setting up the infusion), or 0.05 units/kg/h for mild DKA — and if a nurse-driven variable-rate protocol is used in DKA, the rate should be no less than 1 unit/h to allow the acidosis to resolve.

Titration principles that hold across all protocols

  • Titrate on the trend, not the number. A glucose of 190 falling from 300 needs a different action than a glucose of 190 rising from 150. Every validated protocol incorporates the rate of change.
  • Rate changes scale with the current rate. A patient running 12 units/h needs a bigger absolute adjustment than one running 1 unit/h; published protocols use increments ranging from 0.5 to 10 units/h depending on the current rate.
  • Decrease rather than stop. The Yale protocol's specific rule: if the glucose drifts into 75–99 mg/dL but has fallen only 1–25 mg/dL since the last check, decrease the infusion — do not stop it. Stopping and restarting drives exactly the glycemic variability you are trying to eliminate.
  • Never run the drip against an unstable dextrose source. If TPN, tube feeds or a dextrose infusion changes, the insulin rate must change with it — ideally in the same order.
  • If the patient is eating while still on the drip, ADA 2026 recommends giving prandial coverage as subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin rather than chasing the meal with the infusion rate — this prevents the large swings in IV requirement and the subsequent hypoglycemia.

Hypoglycemia on the drip

Representative nurse-managed protocol thresholds — cutoffs vary between institutions; use yours.

GlucoseAction
<100 mg/dLTurn the infusion off. Recheck hourly until glucose is above target, then restart at 50% of the previous rate.
<80 mg/dLDiscontinue the infusion and give D50 12.5 g (25 mL) IV. Recheck the glucose every 20 minutes.
<60 mg/dL, or persistently lowRepeat dextrose and activate the institutional hypoglycemia protocol. Look for the cause: interrupted feeds, a stopped steroid, weaning pressors, new renal failure, or adrenal insufficiency.
The commonest cause of hypoglycemia on an insulin drip is not the drip — it is something else that stopped. Feeds held for a procedure, TPN finished, a dextrose-containing antibiotic diluent changed, a steroid dose skipped, or pressors weaned. Before you blame the protocol, read the last 6 hours of the MAR and the nutrition orders.
Transition

IV → subcutaneous transition

➡️

The highest-risk 4 hours of the admission

ADA 2026 §16
Give subcutaneous basal insulin 2 hours BEFORE the infusion is stopped. ADA 2026 states this directly: "Subcutaneous basal insulin should be given 2 h before intravenous infusion is discontinued, with the aim of minimizing rebound hyperglycemia while the subcutaneous insulin achieves its effect." Glargine takes 3–4 hours to reach effect; IV insulin disappears in minutes. Stop the drip without an overlap and you create an insulin-free window — which in type 1 diabetes precipitates DKA within hours. In DKA/HHS transitions specifically, ADA advises basal insulin 2–4 h before, or continuing the IV infusion for 1–2 h after the subcutaneous dose is given.

When to transition

  • Off vasopressors, or nearly so, with reasonable peripheral perfusion (so subcutaneous insulin will actually absorb).
  • Glucose stable within target on a stable infusion rate for at least 6 hours.
  • Eating, or on a stable and predictable nutrition plan (tube feeds or TPN at a fixed rate).
  • If DKA: the acidosis has resolved — venous pH >7.3 or bicarbonate >18 mmol/L and ketones <0.6 mmol/L — and the patient can eat and drink. Do not transition on the glucose alone.

Calculating the subcutaneous dose

ADA 2026 lists three acceptable methods: a weight-based approach, the prior home insulin dose, or extrapolation from the infusion rate. For the extrapolation method the guideline is specific:

average stable rate over the last 6–8 h (U/h)× 24 h= extrapolated 24 h requirement× ~60%= subcutaneous TDD → 50% basal / 50% prandial

Why reduce it at all? ADA 2026: "If calculating from the insulin infusion rate, about 60% of the calculated total daily dose should be used to account for glucotoxicity." The patient's insulin resistance was inflated by the very hyperglycemia you have now corrected — as glucotoxicity resolves, the requirement falls. Other published protocols use 70–80%; the more conservative the patient (elderly, CKD, resolving sepsis, weaning steroids), the closer to 60% you should be.

Then split it the usual way: 50% as basal (given ≥2 h before stopping the drip), 50% as prandial divided across meals — or held entirely if the patient is not eating, in which case give basal plus correction only (§16.8b, Grade A). Add a correction scale sized to the new TDD.

ADA 2026 also notes an emerging alternative: giving a low dose of basal analog (0.15–0.3 units/kg) alongside the IV infusion early in the course may shorten the infusion duration and length of stay and prevent rebound hyperglycemia without increasing hypoglycemia — particularly useful in type 1 diabetes, where any interruption of the drip risks DKA.

Worked example — coming off the drip

Mr. D, 90 kg, day 4 of septic shock from pyelonephritis. Norepinephrine was stopped this morning. He is extubated, eating clears, and his insulin drip has run steadily at 2.5 units/h for the past 8 hours with glucose 150–175 mg/dL. Creatinine has improved to 1.3. He has type 2 diabetes; home regimen was metformin only.

  1. Is he ready? Off pressors ✓, stable rate ≥6 h ✓, eating ✓. Yes.
  2. Extrapolate: 2.5 units/h × 24 h = 60 units over 24 hours.
  3. Apply the glucotoxicity correction: 60 × 0.6 = 36 units subcutaneous TDD. (Cross-check against weight: 36 ÷ 90 kg = 0.4 U/kg/day — squarely inside ADA's 0.3–0.6 range. The two methods agreeing is reassuring; if they disagree by more than ~30%, take the lower.)
  4. Basal = 50% = glargine 18 units — give it now, and stop the drip in 2 hours.
  5. Prandial = 50% = 18 units ÷ 3 = 6 units of lispro with each meal — but he is only on clears, so hold prandial doses until he is eating solid trays, and give correction q4h in the meantime.
  6. Correction: TDD 36 units → under 40 → the sensitive scale.
  7. Check glucose q2h for the first 6 hours after stopping the drip — this is the window where rebound hyperglycemia or an unrecognized gap shows up.
  8. Anticipate the fall. His sepsis is resolving and pressors are off; his requirement will keep dropping. Review the numbers in 24 h and expect to reduce, not increase. At discharge, with an A1c that was 6.9%, he will likely go back to metformin alone.

🧮 IV drip → subcutaneous transition calculator

Implements ADA Standards of Care 2026 §16: extrapolate the total daily dose from the stable infusion rate over the last 6–8 h, apply the glucotoxicity correction (ADA specifies ~60%; some protocols use up to 80%), then split 50% basal / 50% prandial. Cross-checked against the weight-based 0.3–0.6 U/kg/day range.

Special

Special ICU situations

⚙️

Circumstances that change the plan

SituationEffect on glucose & insulinWhat to do
Vasopressors being weanedCatecholamines drive glycogenolysis and suppress insulin release. As they come off, requirement falls steeply.Pre-emptively reduce the infusion rate as the pressor comes down, and increase glucose check frequency. This is a leading cause of ICU hypoglycemia.
Continuous renal replacement therapyGlucose in the replacement/dialysate fluid adds a carbohydrate load; conversely, glucose-free solutions remove glucose. Insulin clearance also changes.Know the dialysate glucose concentration. Recheck glucose q1h for several hours after any change in CRRT prescription.
Therapeutic hypothermia / targeted temperature managementCooling causes insulin resistance and hyperglycemia; rewarming reverses it abruptly.Expect requirements to fall sharply during rewarming — reduce the rate proactively.
Cardiac surgeryCardiopulmonary bypass, hypothermia and high-dose steroids all raise glucose intraoperatively.§16.5a permits 110–140 mg/dL in selected cardiac surgery patients. GLUCO-CABG suggests the benefit is concentrated in patients without known diabetes.
Patient on an SGLT2 inhibitor admitted to ICUEuglycemic DKA risk — glucose may be normal while the anion gap widens.Hold the drug, check β-hydroxybutyrate and a gas, and treat with insulin plus dextrose if ketotic with a normal glucose. Emergency surgery on an SGLT2 inhibitor requires close post-op DKA surveillance.
Type 1 diabetes in the ICUAny interruption of insulin causes DKA within hours — there is no endogenous reserve.Never allow an insulin-free interval. Consider concurrent low-dose basal analog (0.15–0.3 U/kg) alongside the infusion. Build an EHR alert so basal is not "held" during transfers.
Steroid pulse (e.g. methylprednisolone)Requirement can double within 12–24 h and then fall as fast when the pulse ends.An infusion handles this far better than subcutaneous insulin. Reduce proactively when the pulse finishes.
Prolonged NPO on the dripBasal glucose needs are unmet; ketosis can develop even in type 2 diabetes.Run a dextrose-containing maintenance fluid (D5 or D10) alongside the insulin so you are titrating insulin against a known, steady carbohydrate input rather than against starvation.
Downgrade

When to downgrade to the floor

⬇️

De-escalation criteria

Ready for the floor when all of these hold:
  • Off the insulin infusion for at least 4–6 hours on a subcutaneous regimen, with glucose staying in range.
  • Basal insulin was given ≥2 hours before the drip was stopped, and the overlap is documented.
  • No hypoglycemia (<70 mg/dL) in the preceding 12–24 hours.
  • Glucose 140–180 mg/dL (or 100–180 once on the floor) without needing hourly adjustment.
  • Off vasopressors, hemodynamically stable, with adequate peripheral perfusion for reliable subcutaneous absorption.
  • Nutrition plan is stable and defined — eating, or on a fixed-rate feed with matched insulin and a written feed-interruption order.
  • If DKA: resolved — venous pH >7.3 or bicarbonate >18 mmol/L and ketones <0.6 mmol/L; if HHS: effective osmolality <300 mOsm/kg, glucose <250, urine output >0.5 mL/kg/h.
  • Electrolytes corrected and stable — particularly K⁺, magnesium and phosphate.
  • The receiving floor can perform glucose checks at the required frequency.
Not yet — hold the transfer if: the anion gap is still open or ketones remain ≥0.6 mmol/L (regardless of how good the glucose looks); the patient came off the drip less than 4 hours ago; there was any hypoglycemia in the last 12 hours; pressors are still running; the nutrition plan is about to change (feeds starting, TPN stopping, extubation and diet advance pending); steroids are being tapered without a matching insulin plan; or nobody has written the subcutaneous regimen and the floor team would inherit a patient with no scheduled insulin at all.
The transfer note is a clinical intervention. Hand off, in writing: the drip rate at the time of transition, the calculated subcutaneous TDD and how you derived it, the exact time basal was given, the current correction scale, the nutrition plan, and what you expect the requirement to do next ("expect to fall as steroids taper — reduce basal 20% when prednisone drops to 20 mg"). Care transitions are where basal insulin gets silently dropped, and ADA specifically recommends practice alerts to prevent it.
Pearls

Clinical pearls

💡

What actually changes management on rounds

  1. Send the admission A1c on day 1. It is the single test that classifies the patient (known / undiagnosed / stress hyperglycemia) and determines the discharge regimen. §16.1, Grade B. Ordering it on day 4 is ordering it too late to be useful.
  2. Never hold basal insulin in type 1 diabetes. Not when NPO, not for a procedure, not when the glucose is 90, not during a transfer. Omission causes DKA within hours. Correction-only insulin is explicitly contraindicated in type 1 diabetes.
  3. A fasting glucose under 100 is a warning, not a win. ADA cites it as a predictor of hypoglycemia within 24 hours that "necessitates basal insulin dose adjustments." Cut the basal 10–20% that morning.
  4. Read the pattern, not the last number. High fasting = basal problem. High after meals with normal fasting = prandial problem. High everywhere = whole regimen underdosed, or a new precipitant. Escalating basal to fix post-meal numbers ("over-basalization") causes nocturnal hypoglycemia without fixing the day.
  5. Roll the correction insulin into tomorrow's scheduled doses. If a patient needed 14 units of correction over 24 hours, that is 14 units the scheduled regimen should have delivered. This is the highest-yield daily titration move there is.
  6. Morning prednisone gives a normal fasting glucose and a terrible dinner glucose. The answer is NPH at 8 AM with the steroid — dosed 0.1 U/kg per 10 mg of prednisone, up to 0.4 U/kg at ≥40 mg — not more basal.
  7. When the steroid comes down, the insulin comes down the same day. ADA lists abrupt corticosteroid reduction among the leading causes of iatrogenic inpatient hypoglycemia. Write the insulin taper on the same order as the steroid taper.
  8. Give basal insulin two hours before you stop the drip. Glargine needs 3–4 hours to work; IV insulin is gone in minutes. The gap between them is where DKA happens.
  9. When extrapolating a subcutaneous dose from a drip rate, take about 60% of it. Glucotoxicity inflated the requirement; as the hyperglycemia resolves so does the resistance. Then cross-check against 0.3–0.6 U/kg/day — if the two methods disagree substantially, take the lower.
  10. Prime the insulin tubing with 20 mL. Unprimed PVC tubing adsorbs enough insulin that only ~84% of the ordered dose reaches the patient. A "non-responding" drip in the first hour may just be under-delivered.
  11. Hypoglycemia is almost never a surprise. 84% of severe episodes (<40 mg/dL) were preceded by a milder low in the same admission, 78% happened in patients on basal insulin, and the peak time is midnight to 6 AM. Yet 75% had no basal dose change before the next dose. Treat the low, then change the regimen — §16.13 makes it mandatory.
  12. Glucagon fails in exactly the patients who need it most. It works by mobilizing hepatic glycogen, so it is unreliable in starvation, alcohol use, cirrhosis, prolonged fasting, and adrenal insufficiency — and it is useless in sulfonylurea hypoglycemia, where it provokes more insulin release. Get IV access and give dextrose; consider octreotide for sulfonylurea overdose.
  13. A patient on an SGLT2 inhibitor who feels unwell needs a ketone level, not reassurance from the glucose. Euglycemic DKA accounts for roughly 10% of all DKA and presents with a glucose under 200. Check β-hydroxybutyrate and the anion gap.
  14. Serum β-hydroxybutyrate beats urine ketones. Dipsticks measure acetoacetate: falsely mild early in DKA, and falsely alarming during recovery as β-OHB converts back to acetoacetate. Never chase a "worsening" urine ketone in an improving patient.
  15. Correct the sodium before you diagnose hyponatremia. Add 1.6 mEq/L per 100 mg/dL of glucose above 100 (2.4 if glucose >400). Most "hyponatremia" in a hyperglycemic patient is translocational and needs insulin, not hypertonic saline.
  16. Watch the potassium fall as you treat. Insulin drives K⁺ intracellularly. A "normal" K⁺ in a hyperglycemic, osmotically diuresing patient usually conceals a large total-body deficit.
  17. Regular insulin, not a rapid analog, is the tube-feed insulin. Its 6–8 hour duration matches continuous carbohydrate delivery, and ADA notes a regular-based plan achieved better control with fewer injections. And never target below 140 mg/dL on continuous feeds.
  18. Write the feed-interruption order at the same time you write the feed order. "If enteral feeds held, start D10 and check glucose q1–2h." Feeds get held for imaging, high residuals and tube displacement constantly — the insulin does not know.
  19. Put the insulin in the TPN bag. Start at 1 unit of regular insulin per 10 g of dextrose. ADA calls it the safest approach precisely because the insulin stops at the same instant the glucose does if the bag is interrupted.
  20. Convert premixed insulins on admission. A fixed 70/30 ratio cannot be unbundled when a meal is missed, and randomized inpatient data show significantly more hypoglycemia than basal-bolus.
  21. U-500 insulin requirements fall by up to 75% in hospital regardless of pre-admission control. Pen or pharmacy-drawn only, and call endocrine.
  22. Degludec given before admission is still working two days later. Do not stack a new full basal dose on top; reduce early, because you cannot hold it off retroactively.
  23. Sliding-scale-alone fails one patient in five. In the Basal Plus trial, 19% of SSI patients met treatment failure (>2 consecutive glucoses >240) versus 0–2% on scheduled regimens. And in RABBIT-2, 14% of SSI patients never got below 240 despite escalating doses.
  24. Basal-plus-correction is a legitimate simplification. The Basal Plus trial showed once-daily glargine plus pre-meal correction performed as well as full basal-bolus — useful for the patient with erratic intake, and much easier to hand off to a SNF.
  25. Dose prandial insulin after the tray when intake is unreliable. Giving rapid-acting insulin immediately after a meal, sized to what was actually eaten, is safer than pre-dosing a tray that gets sent back untouched.
  26. Check the injection sites. Lipohypertrophy from repeated injection into the same spot causes erratic absorption and is a genuinely common, entirely invisible cause of unexplained glucose swings.
  27. Unexplained hyperglycemia is often the first sign of a new infection. If the insulin requirement climbs without a medication change, look for a source before you simply increase the dose.
  28. Consult the diabetes team. §16.3, Grade B — specialist and virtual glucose management services reduced both hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia by 30–40%, shortened length of stay, and cut 30-day readmissions.
  29. Prescribe the needles. An insulin prescription without pen needles or syringes is the most common preventable discharge failure in this disease. Same for strips, lancets, and a glucagon kit.
  30. Ask what it will cost them. A regimen the patient cannot afford is a readmission with extra steps. Human NPH and regular insulin remain a legitimate, far cheaper fallback — accept the modestly higher hypoglycemia risk and teach the timing carefully.

  • ADA. "Summary of Revisions: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026." Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl. 1):S6–S12. — Documents the 2026 changes to §16: new Rec 16.14 (preoperative A1C <8%) and Rec 16.15 (perioperative glucose 100–180 mg/dL), the update to Rec 16.18 on discharge facility capabilities, and new Tables 16.1/16.2 for DKA/HHS. doi.org/10.2337/dc26-SREV
  • ADA. "6. Glycemic Goals, Hypoglycemia, and Hyperglycemic Crises: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026." Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl. 1):S132. — Source for the level 1/2/3 hypoglycemia classification (Table 6.4). full text
  • Korytkowski MT, et al. "Management of Hyperglycemia in Hospitalized Adult Patients in Non-Critical Care Settings: An Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline." J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2022;107(8):2101–2128. — Source for Recs 1.1–10.3 quoted in this guide, including the single strong recommendation (10.3, continue the scheduled insulin regimen modified for nutritional status and illness severity), the DPP-4 inhibitor criteria (Rec 7.2), correctional-insulin thresholds (Recs 10.1–10.2), and glucocorticoid/enteral-nutrition guidance (Recs 2.1, 6.1). academic.oup.com · PMID 35690958
  • Umpierrez GE, et al. "Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report." ADA/EASD/AACE/DTS/JBDS 2024 — the source ADA 2026 adapts for Figure 16.1 and Tables 16.1/16.2 (DKA/HHS criteria and treatment pathways). See the dedicated DKA and HHS guides in this library.
  • U.S. Preventive Services Task Force — Grade A and B recommendation statements (prediabetes/type 2 diabetes screening in adults 35–70 with overweight/obesity; statin, hypertension, tobacco, obesity, and behavioral counseling recommendations). uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org
  • American College of Radiology, ACR Manual on Contrast Media — current metformin guidance (hold only for eGFR <30, suspected AKI, or intra-arterial contrast with likely renal exposure; re-check renal function before restarting). acr.org/Clinical-Resources/Contrast-Manual

Landmark trials

TrialYearDesign / nKey resultWhy it matters
Leuven-1
Van den Berghe, NEJM		2001 RCT, n=1,548 surgical ICU patients on mechanical ventilation. Intensive 80–110 vs conventional (insulin only >215, target 180–200). ICU mortality 4.6% vs 8.0% (P<0.04); ICU stay >5 days 10.6% vs 20.2% (P=0.005). Bloodstream infection ↓46%, dialysis-requiring AKI ↓41%, polyneuropathy ↓44%. Launched the tight-glycemic-control era. PMID 11794168
Leuven-2
Van den Berghe, NEJM		2006 RCT, n=1,200 medical ICU patients, same targets. In-hospital mortality 37.3% vs 40.0%, NS (P=0.33). Morbidity improved. Mortality was higher with intensive control in those staying <3 days; benefit only at ≥3 days (52.5%→43.0%, P=0.009). Showed the surgical-ICU benefit did not generalize. PMID 16452557
RABBIT-2
Umpierrez, Diabetes Care		2007 RCT, n=130 insulin-naive non-ICU medical inpatients with T2DM. Glargine+glulisine (0.4 U/kg if BG 140–200; 0.5 U/kg if BG 201–400, split 50/50) vs sliding-scale regular insulin QID. Target BG <140 reached in 66% vs 38%; mean glucose 27 mg/dL lower (166 vs 193 mg/dL, P<0.01). 14% of SSI patients never got below 240 despite escalating doses. No difference in hypoglycemia or LOS. The foundational trial against sliding-scale-only insulin, and the source of the weight-based starting doses. PMID 17513708
NICE-SUGAR
NEJM		2009 RCT, n=6,104 medical + surgical ICU patients. Intensive 81–108 vs conventional ≤180 mg/dL; 90-day mortality. Intensive control increased mortality: 27.5% vs 24.9% (OR 1.14, 95% CI 1.02–1.28, P=0.02). Severe hypoglycemia (≤40) 6.8% vs 0.5% (P<0.001). Ended tight glycemic control; established today's ICU target of 140–180 mg/dL. PMID 19318384
RABBIT-2 Surgery
Umpierrez, Diabetes Care		2011 RCT, n=211 general-surgery patients with T2DM. Basal-bolus 0.5 U/kg (0.3 U/kg if age ≥70 or Cr ≥2.0) vs SSI QID. Mean glucose 145±32 vs 172±47 mg/dL (P<0.01). Composite complications 8.6% vs 24.3% (OR 3.39, 95% CI 1.50–7.65, P=0.003); wound infection 2.9% vs 10.3% (P=0.05). Hypoglycemia <70 was higher with basal-bolus (23.1% vs 4.7%), but <40 did not differ (P=0.057). Moved the argument from glucose numbers to hard clinical outcomes, and is the source of the age/creatinine dose-reduction rule. PMID 21228246
Basal Plus
Umpierrez, Diabetes Care		2013 RCT, n=375 medical and surgical inpatients. Basal-bolus vs basal + correction only vs SSI. Basal-plus ≈ basal-bolus. Treatment failure 0% vs 2% vs 19% (P<0.001). BG <70 in 16% vs 13% vs 3% (P=0.02); no difference in severe hypoglycemia <40 (P=0.76). Validates the simpler basal-plus-correction regimen — useful when intake is erratic or hand-off capacity is limited. PMID 23435159
GLUCO-CABG
Umpierrez, Diabetes Care		2015 RCT, n=302 post-CABG. Intensive 100–140 vs conservative 141–180 mg/dL. Composite complications 42% vs 52%, NS (P=0.08). With diabetes: 49% vs 48% (P=0.87). Without diabetes: 34% vs 55% (P=0.008). Underpins §16.5a's allowance of 110–140 mg/dL in selected cardiac surgery patients. PMID 26180108
Sita-Hospital
Pasquel, Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol		2017 Multicentre open-label non-inferiority RCT, n=277 general medicine/surgery inpatients with T2DM (BG 140–400 mg/dL, prior insulin ≤0.6 U/kg/day). Sitagliptin + basal glargine vs basal-bolus. Non-inferior: mean daily glucose 171 vs 169 mg/dL (difference 0.1 mmol/L, 95% CI −0.6 to 0.7). Treatment failure 16% vs 19% (P=0.54); hypoglycemia 9% vs 12% (P=0.45); no deaths. The evidence base for using a DPP-4 inhibitor plus basal insulin in mild-to-moderate inpatient hyperglycemia. PMID 27964837
Umpierrez epidemiology study
JCEM		2002 Retrospective review of 2,030 consecutive adult admissions. Hyperglycemia in 38% (26% known diabetes, 12% newly recognized). In-hospital mortality 16% with new hyperglycemia vs 3% with known diabetes vs 1.7% with normoglycemia; longer LOS, more ICU admissions, less likely discharged home. The prevalence and prognostic data that motivated inpatient glycemic protocols. PMID 11889147
Yale Insulin Infusion Protocol
Goldberg, Diabetes Care		2004 Implementation study of a nurse-run IV insulin protocol in a medical ICU; standard 1 U/mL concentration. Established the widely copied architecture: initiation by glucose ÷ 100, titration by both current glucose and its rate of change, hourly monitoring until stable. Updated in 2012 (Shetty, Endocr Pract) to a 120–160 mg/dL target with hypoglycemia <70 in only 0.3% of values. The template for most institutional insulin infusion protocols. Diabetes Care 2004;27:461 · PMID 22138078 (2012 update)

Supporting references used for specific numbers

  • Insulin onset / peak / duration table — Merck Manual Professional Edition, "Onset, Peak, and Duration of Action of Insulin Preparations." merckmanuals.com
  • Steroid-indexed basal/NPH conversion table (prednisone ≥40/30/20/10 mg → 0.4/0.3/0.2/0.1 U/kg/day; dexamethasone equivalents; timing of glucocorticoid-induced hyperglycemia 3–4 h post-dose lasting 12–16 h) — "Glucocorticoid-Induced Hyperglycemia: A Neglected Problem," Endocrinology and Metabolism. e-enm.org
  • Correction (supplemental) insulin scale, weight-based TDD modifiers, tube-feed and TPN insulin arithmetic, basal titration increments, hypoglycemia treatment doses — Endotext, "Inpatient Diabetes Management" (NCBI Bookshelf, NBK278972). ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK278972
  • Weight-based starting-dose modifiers by renal function and body habitus; oral agent hold rules — "Glucose Management in Hospitalized Patients," American Family Physician 2017;96(10):648–654. aafp.org
  • Hospital hyperglycemia overview, 0.3–0.5 U/kg starting dose and the >0.6–0.8 U/kg three-fold hypoglycemia signal — Endotext, "Management of Diabetes and Hyperglycemia in Hospitalized Patients" (NBK279093). ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK279093
  • Glucagon dosing (1 mg IM/SC/IV for adults >25 kg, repeat once after 15 min; nasal glucagon 3 mg one spray one nostril) — FDA prescribing information via DailyMed. dailymed.nlm.nih.gov
  • Nurse-managed IV insulin protocol thresholds and the multiplier architecture — "Evaluation of a Nurse-Managed Insulin Infusion Protocol." PMC4808278; computerized Yale protocol and hypoglycemia analysis, PMC3696925

Calculators — verified live here vs linked out

  • Built live in this guide (arithmetic fully traceable to a cited source): weight-based TDD / basal-bolus starter (ADA 2026 §16 + RABBIT-2), correction factor and correction dose (1800/1500/500 rules), steroid NPH add-on (published prednisone-indexed conversion table), and the IV drip → subcutaneous transition (ADA 2026 §16 extrapolation with the ~60% glucotoxicity correction).
  • Linked out rather than reimplemented — scores whose exact coefficients could not be verified from a primary source, or which are nomogram-based: MDCalc — sodium correction · MDCalc — serum osmolality/osmolarity · MDCalc — anion gap · MDCalc — HOMA-IR · MDCalc — estimated average glucose from A1c

Scope note. This guide covers inpatient hyperglycemia and diabetes management. Diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state have their own dedicated guides in this library and are referenced here only for recognition, escalation criteria and transition rules. Outpatient chronic type 2 diabetes management is covered in the Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus guide.

Educational use only. Doses, thresholds and protocols are traceable to the sources cited above and were verified against the primary literature where possible; institutional protocols differ and always govern. Verify every dose against your local formulary and protocol before acting.
